What is the minimum value of the data set?
questions.whyCorrect: Only the Value column holds data; the Frequency column just says how many times each value appears. The smallest value listed is 13, and it does occur (frequency 8), so the minimum is 13.

whyWrong.A: 1 is the smallest frequency, not the smallest value.
whyWrong.B: 8 is a frequency, not a value in the data set.
whyWrong.D: 20 is in the data set but 13 is smaller.

questions.stem: A botanist estimates the number of oak trees in a forest to be at least 2600 and no more than 3200. Which inequality best represents the number of oak trees, x, in the forest?
questions.whyCorrect: "At least 2600" is a lower bound and "no more than 3200" is an upper bound, so both endpoints are included and the count sits between them.

whyWrong.A: 600 is the width of the range, 3200 - 2600, not a bound on the number of trees.
whyWrong.B: This says there are at most 2600 trees, but 2600 is the smallest possible count.
whyWrong.D: This is the complement of the correct range — it describes every value outside the estimate rather than inside it.

questions.stem: \[ h(t) = -4.9t^{2} + 10t \] The function h models the height \( h(t) \) , in meters, of a football t seconds after it is kicked. What is the interpretation of \( h(2) = 0.40 \) in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The football has a maximum height of 0.40 meter

choices.label: B
choices.content: The football has a maximum height of 2 meters

choices.label: C
choices.content: The football has a height of 0.40 meter 2 seconds after it is kicked

choices.label: D
choices.content: The football has a height of 2 meters 0.40 second after it is kicked

questions.whyCorrect: In \( h(2) = 0.40 \) the number inside the parentheses is the input, which the stem defines as time in seconds, and the number on the right is the output, the height in meters. So at 2 seconds the ball is 0.40 meter up.

whyWrong.A: A single output value says nothing about the maximum. This ball peaks near t = 1 second at about 5 meters, and 0.40 meter is where it is on the way back down.
whyWrong.B: This calls the input a height and also calls it a maximum. 2 is a time.
whyWrong.D: This swaps input and output, reading 2 as a height and 0.40 as a time.

questions.stem: For the function f, for every increase of 2 in the value of x, the value of f(x) increases by a factor of c, where c is a constant. Which of the following equivalent forms of function f displays the value of c as the base of the exponential?
questions.whyCorrect: All four expressions are the same function, \( f(x) = 26(64)^{x} \) , so you cannot choose by simplifying — you have to match the form to the step size. Raising x by 2 multiplies f by \( 64^{2} = 4096 \) , so c = 4096. The base shows the factor per unit of whatever is in the exponent, and only in choice D is the exponent \( \frac{x}{2} \) , which counts steps of 2 — so its base 4096 is the per-2-step factor c.

whyWrong.A: The exponent 6x counts sixths of a unit of x, so the base 2 is the factor per increase of \( \frac{1}{6} \) in x, not per increase of 2.
whyWrong.B: The exponent 2x means the base 8 is the factor per increase of \( \frac{1}{2} \) in x.
whyWrong.C: The exponent is x, so 64 is the factor for an increase of 1 in x. Doubling the step squares it to 4096.

questions.note: The book writes "the base of the coefficient"; read as "the base of the exponential", which is what the choices display.

questions.stem: The graph of a system of two linear equations is shown. If a third equation, x + 2y = -8, is added to this system, how many solutions will the resulting system of three equations have?
questions.whyCorrect: A solution of the three-equation system has to satisfy all three at once, so start from the point where the two graphed lines cross and test it in the new equation. That point does not satisfy \(x + 2y = -8\). In fact the new line is parallel to one of the graphed lines (same \(x + 2y\) form, different constant), so it never meets it anywhere — there is no common point at all.

whyWrong.B: One solution would need the new line to pass through the existing intersection point. Substituting that point into \(x + 2y = -8\) does not work.
whyWrong.C: Straight lines cannot give two common points unless they coincide, in which case there would be infinitely many.
whyWrong.D: Infinitely many would require all three equations to describe the same line, and the graphed lines already have different slopes.

questions.note: Depends on a coordinate-grid figure that cannot be reproduced as a table. Reading the printed graph, the two lines are the horizontal line y = -4 and the line x + 2y = -2 (through about (-10,4) and (10,-6)), so they meet at (6,-4); that point fails x + 2y = -8, and the new line is parallel to x + 2y = -2. The figure must be supplied before this question ships.
questions.imageAlt: Two straight lines drawn on a square grid in the xy-plane; both axes run from -10 to 10.

questions.stem:
\[ f(x) = 3(x - a)(x - b)(x - c) \]The function f is defined by the given equation, where a, b, and c are distinct constants. When \( a < x < b \) , the value of f(x) is positive. The graph of y = f(x) in the xy-plane contains the point (r, s), where r and s are constants. If s = 8, which of the following could be true?

I. \( r < a \)
II. \( b < r < c \)
III. \( r > c \)
questions.whyCorrect: First pin down the order of the three roots. The leading coefficient 3 is positive, so a cubic with three distinct roots is negative below the smallest root, positive between the smallest and middle, negative between the middle and largest, and positive above the largest. You are told f is positive on the whole interval from a to b, so no root sits inside it and (a, b) must be the smallest-to-middle gap: the order is a, then b, then c. Since s = 8 is positive, r must lie where f is positive, which is between a and b or above c. Only statement III describes such a region.

whyWrong.A: Below the smallest root a the cubic is negative, so f(r) could not equal 8. Statement I is never possible.
whyWrong.C: This adds statement I, which fails for the reason above; only III survives.
whyWrong.D: Between b and c the cubic is negative (that is the middle-to-largest gap), so f(r) = 8 is impossible there. Statement II fails.

questions.stem: \[ F(x) = \frac{9}{5}(x - 273.15) + 32 \]The function \(F\) gives the temperature, in degrees Fahrenheit, that corresponds to x kelvins. If a temperature is increased by 11.70 kelvins, by how much did the temperature increase in degrees Fahrenheit?
questions.whyCorrect: You are asked for a change, not a temperature, so only the rate matters: every 1 kelvin of increase adds \(\frac{9}{5}\) degrees Fahrenheit. The -273.15 and the +32 shift where the scale starts and cancel out of any difference. So the increase is \(\frac{9}{5}(11.70) = 21.06\) degrees Fahrenheit.

questions.stem:
\[ x(x+4)-140=3x(x-10) \]
What is the sum of the solutions to the given equation?
questions.whyCorrect: Expand both sides: \(x^2+4x-140=3x^2-30x\). Collect everything on one side: \(2x^2-34x+140=0\), and dividing by 2 gives \(x^2-17x+70=0\). The sum of the solutions is \(-\frac{b}{a}=17\) (the roots are 7 and 10).

whyWrong.A: 6 is \(10-4\), read straight off the numbers in the stem rather than from the collected equation.
whyWrong.B: 10 is only one of the two solutions; the question asks for their sum.
whyWrong.C: 14 is \(10+4\), again the stem's numbers rather than the roots. The 4 and the 10 are inside brackets that get multiplied out, so they are not the roots.

questions.stem: A school is ordering tablet computers for its students. The tablets cost $164 each, and 6% tax is added to the total cost of the order. If the school can spend no more than 44,800 dollars on the tablets, including tax, what is the maximum number of tablets that the school can order?
questions.whyCorrect: Build the after-tax price per tablet first: 164(1.06) = 173.84 dollars. Then \( 173.84n \le 44{,}800 \) gives \( n \le 257.7 \). Tablets come in whole units and the budget is a ceiling, so round down to 257 rather than up.

questions.stem: By examining pollen in the soil, scientists estimated that the number of Ulmus trees in an ancient population doubled every 664 years. There were \(n\) trees in the earliest known sample, where \(n\) is a constant. Which expression gives the estimated number of Ulmus trees \(x\) years after the year of the earliest known sample?
questions.whyCorrect: In \(n(2)^{t}\), the exponent counts how many doublings have happened. After \(x\) years there have been \(\frac{x}{664}\) doubling periods, so the expression is \(n(2)^{\frac{x}{664}}\). Check it at \(x=664\): the exponent is 1 and the population is \(2n\), exactly one doubling.

whyWrong.A: At \(x=664\) this gives \(n(2)^{441{,}496}\) — it doubles 664 times per year instead of once every 664 years. The period belongs in the denominator.
whyWrong.B: This has \(x\) in the denominator, so growing \(x\) makes the exponent shrink toward 0; the population would decrease over time.
whyWrong.D: Adding \(x\) to 664 makes the population \(n(2)^{664}\) at time zero, which contradicts the starting count of \(n\).

questions.stem: When a collection of books is sorted, 52% are nonfiction and the remaining books are fiction. Of those that are fiction, 75% are westerns and the remaining fiction books are romance. If there are 933 romance books in this collection, what is the total number of books in the collection?
questions.whyCorrect: Track the fractions down to romance. Fiction is \(100\% - 52\% = 48\%\) of the collection, and romance is the \(100\% - 75\% = 25\%\) of fiction that is not westerns. So romance is \(0.48 \times 0.25 = 0.12\) of the whole collection. Then \(0.12T = 933\) gives \(T = 7{,}775\).

questions.stem: If \[\frac{7}{8}p + 35 = 56,\] what is the value of \(8p\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Subtract 35: \(\frac{7}{8}p = 21\). Multiply by \(\frac{8}{7}\): \(p = 24\). The question asks for \(8p\), so the answer is \(8 \times 24 = 192\).

questions.stem:
\[ -3x^2-7x+1=0 \]
What is the greatest solution to the given equation?
questions.whyCorrect: Multiply through by \(-1\) so the leading coefficient is positive: \(3x^2+7x-1=0\). Then \(x=\frac{-7\pm\sqrt{49+12}}{6}=-\frac{7}{6}\pm\frac{\sqrt{61}}{6}\), and the greatest solution takes the plus sign.

whyWrong.A: The denominator is \(2a=6\), not 3. Using \(a\) instead of \(2a\) doubles both terms.
whyWrong.B: Same denominator error, and it takes the smaller root as well.
whyWrong.D: Correct denominators but the minus sign, which gives the smaller of the two solutions.

questions.stem: The area of a triangle is equal to \(x^2\) square centimeters. The length of the base of the triangle is 2x + 6 centimeters, and the height of the triangle is x − 2 centimeters. What is the value of x?
questions.whyCorrect: Write the area two ways and set them equal: \(x^2 = \frac{1}{2}(2x + 6)(x - 2)\). Halving the base first makes the algebra easy: \(\frac{1}{2}(2x+6) = x + 3\), so the right side is \((x + 3)(x - 2) = x^2 + x - 6\). The \(x^2\) terms cancel, leaving x - 6 = 0, so x = 6 (base 18, height 4, area 36).

questions.stem: A survey was conducted in Franklin to estimate the number of adult residents who supported the addition of a parking garage in their town. Based on the survey, it is estimated that 77% of all adult residents of Franklin support the addition of a parking garage in their town, with an associated margin of error of 5%. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about all adult residents of Franklin?

choices.label: A
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Franklin who support the addition of a parking garage in their town are between 72% and 82%

choices.label: B
choices.content: The addition of a parking garage in the town is supported by exactly 72% of all adult residents of Franklin

choices.label: C
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Franklin who support the addition of a parking garage in their town are either less than 72% or more than 82%

choices.label: D
choices.content: The addition of a parking garage in the town is supported by more than 82% of all adult residents of Franklin

questions.whyCorrect: Subtract and add the margin of error: 77 − 5 = 72 and 77 + 5 = 82. The survey supports the claim that the true percentage lies somewhere in that band, and says nothing more precise than that.

whyWrong.B: 72% is the low end of the interval, not a value the survey singles out, and a sample never establishes an exact population percentage.
whyWrong.C: This names everything outside the interval — the values the survey argues against, not for.
whyWrong.D: 82% is the top of the interval, so support above it is what the estimate rules out as unlikely.

questions.stem: If (x + 9) − 5 = 25, what is the value of x + 9?
questions.whyCorrect: Treat \(x+9\) as a single block: adding 5 to both sides gives \(x + 9 = 30\) immediately. There is no need to find \(x\) (which is 21).

whyWrong.B: 21 is the value of \(x\), not \(x+9\). The question asks for the whole expression.
whyWrong.C: 20 is \(25-5\); the 5 is being subtracted on the left, so undoing it means adding 5 to 25.
whyWrong.D: 11 comes from subtracting 9 as well and mixing up which quantity is being asked for.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to \( (158y)^{\frac{1}{2}} \) , where \( y > 1 \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: An exponent of \( \frac{1}{2} \) is a square root, and the parentheses mean the whole product 158y is raised to that power. So the expression is \( \sqrt{158y} \) .

whyWrong.A: Here the root is applied only to y, leaving the 158 outside. The parentheses put both inside.
whyWrong.B: The mirror-image error — the root applied only to the 158.
whyWrong.D: Squaring first and then taking the root undoes both operations, giving 158y itself, which is the expression raised to the power 1, not \( \frac{1}{2} \) .

questions.stem: The measure of angle \(Z\) is 45°. What is the measure, in <u>radians</u>, of angle \(Z\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Multiply degrees by \(\frac{\pi}{180}\): \(45 \cdot \frac{\pi}{180} = \frac{\pi}{4}\). Another way to see it: 180° is \(\pi\) radians and 45° is a quarter of 180°, so it is a quarter of \(\pi\).

whyWrong.A: \(\frac{\pi}{2}\) is 90°, twice the given angle.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{3\pi}{4}\) is 135°, the supplement of 45°.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{\pi}{8}\) is 22.5° — this divides 180 by 8 instead of by 4.

questions.stem:
The table shows the frequency of each value in a data set.
ValueFrequency
1203
1308
14018
1508
1601
What is the minimum value of the data set?
questions.whyCorrect: The data set consists of the numbers in the Value column; the Frequency column only counts repeats. The smallest value listed is 120, and its frequency of 3 confirms it actually occurs, so the minimum is 120.

whyWrong.A: 1 is the smallest frequency (how often 160 occurs), not a data value.
whyWrong.B: 3 is the frequency of 120, not the value itself.
whyWrong.D: 160 is the maximum value, not the minimum.

questions.stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \[ f(x) = \frac{1}{2}(x + 8). \]What is the value of \(f(10)\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Work inside the parentheses first: 10 + 8 = 18, then halve it to get 9. The \(\frac{1}{2}\) multiplies the whole sum, not just the x.

whyWrong.A: This doubles 18 instead of halving it — multiplying by \(\frac{1}{2}\) is division by 2, not by \(\frac{1}{2}\).
whyWrong.B: 18 is the value inside the parentheses. You still have to multiply by \(\frac{1}{2}\).
whyWrong.C: This halves only the 10 and then adds 8 without halving it, ignoring the parentheses.

questions.stem: At the time of posting a video, a social media channel had 95 subscribers. Each day for five days after the video was posted, the number of subscribers doubled from the previous day. Which equation gives the total number of subscribers, \(n\), to the channel \(d\) days after the video was posted?
questions.whyCorrect: Doubling each day means multiplying by 2 once per day, so 2 is the base and \(d\) the exponent, with the starting 95 as the coefficient: \(n = 95(2)^{d}\). At \(d = 0\) it gives 95 and at \(d = 1\) it gives 190, which is the check.

whyWrong.A: This raises the starting count to the power \(d\); after one day it would predict 95 subscribers, and after two, 9,025.
whyWrong.C: A base of \(\frac{1}{2}\) halves the subscribers each day instead of doubling them.
whyWrong.D: This is not exponential at all — it adds one subscriber per day to a fixed 9,025.

questions.note: Same question as satmath-ma2-exponential-functions-25 with 95 subscribers instead of 88 - do not place both in one test.

questions.stem: Circle T has a radius of 35 millimeters (mm). What is the area of circle T, in mm<sup>2</sup>?
questions.whyCorrect: Area of a circle is \(\pi r^{2}\), so with r = 35 the area is \(\pi(35)^{2} = 1{,}225\pi\) square millimeters. The radius has to be squared, not just multiplied by \(\pi\).

whyWrong.A: This multiplies the radius by \(\pi\) without squaring it.
whyWrong.B: This is \(2\pi r\), the circumference, which is a length rather than an area.
whyWrong.C: This is twice the circumference. It still never squares the radius.

questions.stem: In December 2017, the lowest temperature recorded in a certain city was 40 degrees Fahrenheit (°F) and the highest temperature recorded was 90°F. Which inequality is true for all values of t, where t represents any temperature in °F recorded in the city in December?
questions.whyCorrect: The lowest recorded value is a floor and the highest is a ceiling, so every recorded temperature sits between them, endpoints included. That is written as one double inequality: 40 ≤ t ≤ 90.

whyWrong.B: This says every temperature was at most 40, but 40 was the minimum, so almost all readings were above it.
whyWrong.C: 50 is not mentioned in the problem and nothing caps the readings there — the maximum was 90.
whyWrong.D: This says every temperature was at least 90, but 90 was the maximum, not the minimum.

questions.stem: The ratio of 12 to \(x\) is equal to the ratio of 156 to \(y\). Which expression represents \(y\) in terms of \(x\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Write the two ratios as equal fractions in the same order: \(\frac{12}{x} = \frac{156}{y}\). Cross-multiply to get \(12y = 156x\), then divide by 12: \(y = 13x\). The check is that 156 is 13 times 12, so \(y\) must be 13 times \(x\) for the ratio to hold.

whyWrong.A: This is the reciprocal relationship. Since the first term grew from 12 to 156, the second term must grow too, not shrink.
whyWrong.C: This divides by 12 rather than using the factor between 12 and 156.
whyWrong.D: This uses 12 as the scale factor. The factor linking the two ratios is \(\frac{156}{12} = 13\).

questions.stem: \[ x^{2} - 10x + 24 = 0 \] How many distinct real solutions does the given equation have?
questions.whyCorrect: The discriminant is \( (-10)^{2} - 4(1)(24) = 100 - 96 = 4 \) , which is positive, so there are two distinct real solutions. Factoring confirms it: \( (x - 4)(x - 6) = 0 \) gives x = 4 and x = 6.

whyWrong.A: Exactly one requires a discriminant of 0, which would need the constant term to be 25, not 24. A near-miss like this is why you should compute the discriminant rather than eyeball it.
whyWrong.C: A quadratic equation cannot have infinitely many solutions; a parabola meets a horizontal line in at most two points.
whyWrong.D: Zero solutions requires a negative discriminant, meaning 4ac exceeds \( b^{2} \) . Here 96 is less than 100.

questions.stem:
\[ f(x) = -2x^2+bx+c \]In the given quadratic function, \(b\) and \(c\) are constants. The graph of \( y = f(x) \) is a parabola that has a vertex at the point \( (h,k) \), where \(h\) and \(k\) are constants. If \( k < 0 \) and \( f(-5) = f(7) \), which of the following must be true?
I. \( c < -1 \)
II. \( b \ge 3 \)
questions.whyCorrect: Equal outputs at \( x=-5 \) and \( x=7 \) put the axis of symmetry at their midpoint, \( x = 1 \). So \( -\frac{b}{2(-2)} = \frac{b}{4} = 1 \), fixing \( b = 4 \), which satisfies \( b \ge 3 \). The vertex value is \( k = f(1) = -2+4+c = c+2 \), and \( k < 0 \) gives \( c < -2 \); anything less than \(-2\) is certainly less than \(-1\), so I holds too.

whyWrong.A: II is also forced — the symmetry condition pins \( b = 4 \) exactly, and \( 4 \ge 3 \).
whyWrong.B: I is also forced: \( k = c+2 < 0 \) means \( c < -2 \), which implies \( c < -1 \).
whyWrong.D: Both statements follow; the axis of symmetry gives \(b\) and the vertex value gives the bound on \(c\).

questions.note: Book prints "a and c are constants" though the equation uses b and c; corrected to b and c.

questions.stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \[ f(x) = 9x^2+kx-21 \]where \(k\) is a constant. In the xy-plane, the graph of \( y = f(x) \) passes through the points \( (r,23) \) and \( (2r,139) \), where \(r\) is a constant. Which of the following could be the value of \(k\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Substitute both points: \( 9r^2+kr-21 = 23 \) gives \( 9r^2+kr = 44 \), and \( 36r^2+2kr-21 = 139 \) gives \( 36r^2+2kr = 160 \), i.e. \( 18r^2+kr = 80 \). Subtracting the first from the second eliminates \(k\): \( 9r^2 = 36 \), so \( r = \pm 2 \). Putting \( r = 2 \) back gives \( 36+2k = 44 \), so \( k = 4 \) (and \( r=-2 \) gives \( k=-4 \), which is not offered).

whyWrong.B: 12 does not satisfy either equation; with \( k=12 \) the two conditions give incompatible values of \(r\).
whyWrong.C: 116 is what you get by keeping \( 9r^2+kr = 44 \) and \( 18r^2+kr = 80 \) but solving for \(kr\) instead of \(k\) and forgetting to divide by \(r\).
whyWrong.D: 162 comes from adding the two equations rather than subtracting, which does not eliminate anything usable.

questions.stem:
5x + 7y = 8
30x + 42y = 48

For each real number r, which of the following points lies on the graph of each equation in the xy-plane for the given system?
questions.whyCorrect: The second equation is the first multiplied by 6, so the two graphs are one and the same line and any point on it satisfies both. Let the x-coordinate be the free value r and solve the first equation for y: 5r + 7y = 8 gives \(y = \frac{8 - 5r}{7} = -\frac{5r}{7} + \frac{8}{7}\). That is choice A, and substituting confirms 5x + 7y = 8 for every r.

whyWrong.B: The coordinates are swapped. This expression is the formula for y, but it is placed in the x slot. Substituting gives \(\frac{24r}{7} + \frac{40}{7}\), which equals 8 only for one particular r, not for every r.
whyWrong.C: The constants 8 and 48 are lifted straight from the right-hand sides of the two equations rather than being solved for. Substituting gives \(\frac{10r}{7} + 376\), nowhere near 8.
whyWrong.D: This uses the scale factor 6 as if it belonged in the coordinates. Substituting gives \(376 - \frac{r}{3}\), which is not constant at 8.

questions.stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \[ f(x) = a\sqrt{-x+b} \]where \(a\) and \(b\) are constants. In the xy-plane, the graph of \( y = f(x) \) passes through the point \( (5,0) \), and \( f(-12) > f(-7) \). Which of the following must be true?
questions.whyCorrect: The point \( (5,0) \) forces \( a\sqrt{b-5} = 0 \); \( a = 0 \) would make \(f\) constant and contradict \( f(-12) > f(-7) \), so \( b = 5 \) and \( f(x) = a\sqrt{5-x} \). Since \( \sqrt{17} > \sqrt{12} \), the inequality \( a\sqrt{17} > a\sqrt{12} \) can only hold if \( a > 0 \) — that is all you learn about \(a\). With \( b=5 \), choice C compares \( f(3) = a\sqrt{2} \) with \( f(-10) = a\sqrt{15} \), and a positive \(a\) makes \( a\sqrt{2} < a\sqrt{15} \) always.

whyWrong.A: \( f(b) = f(5) = 0 \), so this says \( a < 0 \) — the opposite of what \( f(-12) > f(-7) \) forces.
whyWrong.B: Nothing bounds the size of \(a\); \( a = 1 \) with \( b = 5 \) satisfies every condition and makes \( a < b \).
whyWrong.D: Equally unforced in the other direction: \( a = 100 \) also satisfies every condition, giving \( a > b \). Only the sign of \(a\) is determined.

questions.stem:
7x + 4y = 3
35x + 20y = 15

For each real number r, which of the following points lies on the graph of each equation in the xy-plane for the given system?
questions.whyCorrect: The second equation is the first multiplied by 5, so both graphs are the same line and any point on that line works. Check which coordinate the choices leave free: here the surviving choice puts r in the y slot, so set y = r and solve 7x + 4r = 3 for x, giving \(x = \frac{3 - 4r}{7} = -\frac{4r}{7} + \frac{3}{7}\). That is choice B, and substituting gives 7x + 4y = 3 for every r.

whyWrong.A: The constants 3 and 15 are copied from the right-hand sides of the two equations instead of being solved for. Substituting gives \(\frac{3r}{5} + 81\), which is not 3.
whyWrong.C: This solves 7r + 4y = 3 for y but drops the minus sign: the correct result is \(-\frac{7r}{4} + \frac{3}{4}\). Substituting the printed version gives 14r + 3.
whyWrong.D: The correct x-expression is placed in the y slot. Substituting gives \(\frac{33r}{7} + \frac{12}{7}\), which equals 3 only at one value of r, not for every r.

questions.stem: The function q is defined by \[ q(x) = a|x - 9|^{2} - 87|x - 9| + b \]where a and b are constants and \( a > b > 87 \) . If q(639) = h and q(-621) = k, where h and k are constants, what is the value of \( 9(-639)^{h-k} + 621(9)^{k-h} \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: The whole function depends on x only through \( |x - 9| \) . For x = 639 that is 630, and for x = -621 it is \( |-630| = 630 \) as well — the two inputs sit the same distance either side of 9. So q gives the same output at both, h = k, and you never need a or b. Then the exponents h - k and k - h are both 0, and any nonzero base to the power 0 is 1, leaving 9(1) + 621(1) = 630.

questions.stem:
6x + 3y = 5

The given equation is one equation in a system of two linear equations. If the system of equations has at least one solution, which of the following equations could be the other equation in the system?

I. 9x + 4.5y = 7.5
II. 9x − 4.5y = 7.5
questions.whyCorrect: "At least one solution" rules out only one case — parallel distinct lines — so both one solution and infinitely many count as acceptable. Equation I is the given equation multiplied by 1.5 throughout (9, 4.5 and 7.5), so it is the same line: infinitely many solutions. Equation II has y-coefficient −4.5 instead of +4.5, so the slopes differ and the lines cross once. Both qualify.

whyWrong.A: This treats "at least one solution" as though it meant infinitely many. A pair of lines that cross at a single point also has at least one solution, and II is exactly that case.
whyWrong.B: This rejects I for being the same line, but a system whose two equations describe one line has infinitely many solutions — which is certainly at least one.
whyWrong.D: Neither equation produces a parallel-distinct pair, which is the only situation with no solution. For that you would need the coefficients to scale by 1.5 while the constant did not.

questions.stem: A development company is advertising that the mean area of the apartments in a new complex is 1,450 square feet. The complex consists of 10 buildings with a total of 1,000 apartments. A sample of 50 apartments will be selected from the complex to test the company's statement about the mean apartment area. Which of the following is an unbiased sampling method?

choices.label: B
choices.content: Select the first 50 apartments that are occupied.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Select at random 5 top-floor apartments from each of the buildings.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Select at random 50 apartments from all the apartments in the 10 buildings.

questions.whyCorrect: A sample is unbiased when every apartment in the complex has the same chance of being chosen. Only D draws at random from all 1,000 apartments; every other method restricts the pool first, so whole categories of apartment can never appear.

whyWrong.A: Build order is not random — the first-built apartments may be a particular size or in particular buildings, and later ones can never be selected.
whyWrong.B: Occupancy is chosen by tenants, and cheaper or smaller units tend to fill first. That preference, not chance, decides the sample.
whyWrong.C: Top-floor apartments are systematically different (often penthouses or larger units), and no other floor can be selected at all. Randomizing within a biased pool does not remove the bias.

questions.stem: The function \[ v(x) = \frac{x^2+bx+c}{(x-7)(x-17)} \]where \(b\), \(c\) are constants goes through the points \( \left(0, \frac{99}{119}\right) \) and \( (11,0) \). There is another point where \( v(q) = 0 \). What is the value of \(q\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Use \( x = 0 \) first, because it kills the \(b\) term: \( v(0) = \frac{c}{(-7)(-17)} = \frac{c}{119} = \frac{99}{119} \), so \( c = 99 \). A fraction is zero only when its numerator is, so \( v(11)=0 \) gives \( 121+11b+99 = 0 \) and \( b = -20 \). The numerator is then \( x^2-20x+99 = (x-9)(x-11) \), so the other zero is \( q = 9 \) — and 9 is not 7 or 17, so it is not cancelled by the denominator.

questions.stem:
22x - 21y = 43
5x + 14y = 59

The solution to the given system of equations is \((x, y) = \left(\frac{p}{59}, \frac{w}{826}\right)\), where \(p\) and \(w\) are integers. What is the value of \(p\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Eliminate \(y\): the coefficients \(-21\) and 14 have least common multiple 42, so multiply the first equation by 2 and the second by 3 and add: \(44x - 42y = 86\) plus \(15x + 42y = 177\) gives \(59x = 263\). That is already in the form \(x = \frac{p}{59}\), so \(p = 263\).

questions.stem: The measure of angle BDC, in radians, is equal to \(\frac{a\pi}{b}\) where a and b are positive integer constants. What is the smallest possible value of \(a + b\)?
questions.whyCorrect: With D at the center, DA, DB and DC are all radii, so triangles ABD and ACD are isosceles and their base angles match the marked ones: \(\angle DAB = \angle DBA = 19^\circ\) and \(\angle DAC = \angle DCA = 19^\circ\). That makes the inscribed angle \(\angle BAC = 38^\circ\), and a central angle is twice the inscribed angle on the same arc, so \(\angle BDC = 76^\circ\). In radians that is \(\frac{76\pi}{180} = \frac{19\pi}{45}\), and in lowest terms \(a + b = 19 + 45 = 64\).
questions.note: DEFECT: the printed stem is only the last sentence — everything else is in the figure, and the figure never states that D is the centre of the circle, which is required to fix the answer. Figure: circle with A on the top arc, B lower left and C lower right on the circle, D marked inside at the centre; segments AB, AC, DB, DC are drawn and the angles ABD and ACD are each marked 19 degrees. Answer 64 assumes D is the centre; without that statement the angle is not determined. | figure: Reproduces the printed figure, which marks D at the centre of the circle but never states that it is the centre - the stem needs that fact to determine the angle. Question flagged as defective on that ground.
questions.imageAlt: Line drawing of a circle with points A, B and C marked on it and point D marked inside; segments join A to B, A to C, D to B and D to C, and two angles are labelled 19 degrees.

questions.stem: A researcher surveyed undergraduate students, graduate students, and postgraduate students. The number of undergraduate students surveyed was 7450% of the number of postdoctoral students surveyed and the number of graduate students surveyed was 24% of the undergraduate students surveyed. If there were 3576 graduate students surveyed, what was the sum of the number of undergraduate students and postdoctoral students surveyed?
questions.whyCorrect: Work backwards from the graduate count. Graduates are 24% of undergraduates, so undergraduates \(= \frac{3576}{0.24} = 14{,}900\). Undergraduates are 7450% of postdoctoral students, and 7450% means 74.5 times, so postdoctoral \(= \frac{14{,}900}{74.5} = 200\). The sum is \(14{,}900 + 200 = 15{,}100\).
questions.note: The stem introduces "postgraduate" students but then asks about "postdoctoral" students; the two are used for the same group.

questions.stem:
The function \[ f(x) = 6(x-a)(x-b)(x-c) \]is defined by the given equation, where \(a\), \(b\), and \(c\) are distinct constants. When \( a < x < b \), the value of \( f(x) \) is positive. The graph of \( y = f(x) \) in the xy-plane contains the point \( (r,s) \), where \(r\) and \(s\) are constants. If \( s = 9 \), which of the following could be true?
I. \( r < a \)
II. \( b < r < c \)
III. \( r > c \)
questions.whyCorrect: First order the zeros. A cubic with positive leading coefficient is negative below its smallest zero, then alternates: positive, negative, positive as \(x\) passes each zero. For \(f\) to be positive on the whole interval \( (a,b) \), that interval must be the first gap, so \( a < b < c \). Then \(f\) is positive exactly on \( (a,b) \) and on \( x > c \). Since \( s = 9 > 0 \), \(r\) has to sit in one of those two regions, and only \( r > c \) appears in the list.

whyWrong.A: For \( r < a \), \(r\) is below the smallest zero, where the cubic is negative — it cannot give \( s = 9 \).
whyWrong.C: III is possible but I is not, for the reason above.
whyWrong.D: On \( b < r < c \) the graph is between the second and third zeros, where a positive-leading cubic is negative, so II is impossible.

questions.stem:
y - x = 32
\(y = x^{2} - 30x\)

The graphs of the equations in the given system intersect at the point \((x, y)\) in the \(xy\)-plane. What is a possible value of \(y\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Rewrite the line as \(y = x + 32\) and set the two expressions for \(y\) equal: \(x + 32 = x^{2} - 30x\), so \(x^{2} - 31x - 32 = 0\), which factors as \((x - 32)(x + 1) = 0\). The intersections are at \(x = 32\) and \(x = -1\), giving \(y = 64\) and \(y = 31\). Only 64 is offered.

whyWrong.A: 32 is the constant in the linear equation and one of the \(x\)-values, not a \(y\)-value of an intersection.
whyWrong.B: 33 is close to the other intersection's \(y\)-value of 31, but not equal to it — check \(x = -1\) carefully.
whyWrong.C: 63 would come from \(x = 31\), which is the coefficient in the quadratic \(x^{2} - 31x - 32\), not a root of it.

questions.stem: \[ak = \frac{b}{12}(7 + m)\]The given equation relates the positive variables \(a\), \(b\), \(k\), and \(m\). Which equation correctly expresses \(m\) in terms of \(a\), \(b\), and \(k\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Undo the multiplication before the addition. Multiply both sides by \(\frac{12}{b}\): \(\frac{12ak}{b} = 7 + m\). Then subtract 7: \(m = \frac{12ak}{b} - 7\).

whyWrong.A: Here 7 was subtracted from \(ak\) before the \(\frac{b}{12}\) was undone; the 7 is inside the bracket, so it can only be removed after dividing by \(\frac{b}{12}\).
whyWrong.B: Dividing by \(\frac{b}{12}\) is not the same as subtracting it, and the bracket was never expanded correctly.
whyWrong.C: This distributes \(\frac{b}{12}\) but then treats \(ak\) as though the \(\frac{b}{12}\) multiplying \(m\) had vanished.

questions.stem: An object is launched from a height of 121 feet above the ground. A quadratic function \(f\) models the height above the ground, in feet, of the object \(t\) seconds after it is launched. According to the model, 2 seconds after the object is launched, it reaches a maximum height of 185 feet above the ground. Which equation defines \(f\)?
questions.whyCorrect: The maximum tells you the vertex: it occurs at time \(t = 2\) with height 185, so the vertex is \((2, 185)\) and the model is \(f(t) = a(t - 2)^2 + 185\). In vertex form the number subtracted from \(t\) is the time and the number added at the end is the height — the order matters. Check the launch height: \(f(0) = -16(4) + 185 = 121\), which matches.

whyWrong.A: The 185 and the 2 have been swapped and both signs are wrong. This puts the vertex at \((-185, -2)\), a negative time and a height below ground.
whyWrong.B: Also swaps the two numbers, putting the maximum height at 2 feet occurring 185 seconds after launch.
whyWrong.C: Keeps the numbers in the right roles but flips both signs, giving a vertex of \((-2, -185)\) — two seconds before launch and 185 feet underground.

questions.stem: A research manager selected 2 random samples of ovens of a certain type to estimate the average amount of time this type of oven takes to preheat to 325 degrees Fahrenheit (°F). The research manager recorded the amount of time, in minutes, each oven takes to preheat to 325°F. Based on the first sample, the research manager estimated that this type of oven takes an average of 15.2 minutes to preheat to 325°F, with an associated margin of error of 1 minute. Based on the second sample, the research manager estimated that this type of oven takes an average of 15.4 minutes to preheat to 325°F, with an associated margin of error of 2.2 minutes. Assuming the margins of error were calculated the same way, which of the following best explains why the first sample obtained a smaller margin of error than the second sample?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The first sample contained more ovens than the second sample.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The first sample contained fewer ovens than the second sample.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The first sample took more time on average to preheat to 325°F than the second sample.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The first sample took less time on average to preheat to 325°F than the second sample.

questions.whyCorrect: With the margins of error calculated the same way, the one that comes out smaller belongs to the larger sample — more data means a more precise estimate. The first sample's margin is 1 minute against the second's 2.2 minutes, so the first sample must have had more ovens in it.

whyWrong.B: This inverts the rule. Fewer ovens would have produced the larger margin of error.
whyWrong.C: The size of the estimated average does not set the margin of error, and it is false here anyway — the first sample's average, 15.2, is the smaller of the two.
whyWrong.D: It is true that 15.2 is less than 15.4, but that difference is not what makes a margin of error small. Only the sample size explains it.

questions.note: Same template as ma2 Research organizing #3 (town manager, 8.3% vs 6.7%); do not place both in one test.

questions.stem: Triangles \(ABC\) and \(DEF\) are congruent, where \(A\) corresponds to \(D\), and \(B\) and \(E\) are right angles. The measure of angle \(A\) is 62°. What is the value of angle \(F\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Track the correspondence: \(A\) matches \(D\) and \(B\) matches \(E\), so the remaining vertices match too — \(C\) with \(F\). Angle \(C\) is what is left in triangle \(ABC\) after the right angle and the 62° angle: \(180 - 90 - 62 = 28^\circ\). Congruence makes angle \(F\) equal to that, 28°.

whyWrong.B: 62° is angle \(D\), the partner of angle \(A\), not of angle \(F\).
whyWrong.C: 90° is angle \(E\), the right angle, which corresponds to \(B\).
whyWrong.D: 118° is 180 − 62, a supplement rather than the third angle of a right triangle.

questions.stem:
Number of carsMaximum number of passengers and crew
4164
6242
8320
The table shows the linear relationship between the number of cars, c, on a commuter train and the maximum number of passengers and crew, p, that the train can carry. Which equation represents the linear relationship between c and p?
questions.whyCorrect: Each extra 2 cars adds 242 − 164 = 78 passengers, so the rate is 39 per car. Then p = 39c + b, and using c = 4: 164 = 156 + b gives b = 8, so p = 39c + 8. Rearranged into the form of the choices, 39c − p = −8. Substituting c = 4 checks it: 156 − 164 = −8.

whyWrong.B: The sign of the constant is flipped. Substituting c = 4, p = 164 gives 156 − 164 = −8, not 8.
whyWrong.C: The variables are swapped, so this says 39 passengers per car in the wrong direction. Substituting gives 39(164) − 4 = 6,392.
whyWrong.D: Same swap with the other sign. It fails the same substitution check; p is the quantity that grows 39 times as fast, so 39 must multiply c.

questions.stem: The height of a right circular cylinder is 6 inches longer than its radius, and the surface area of the cylinder is \(1080\pi\) square inches. What is the cylinder's radius, in inches?
questions.whyCorrect: Write the height as r + 6 and substitute into \(2\pi r^2 + 2\pi rh\): \(2\pi r^2 + 2\pi r(r+6) = 1080\pi\). Divide out \(\pi\) and collect: \(4r^2 + 12r - 1080 = 0\), or \(r^2 + 3r - 270 = 0\), which factors as (r + 18)(r - 15) = 0. A radius cannot be negative, so r = 15 (and the height is 21). Checking with the choices is faster than factoring if you spot it.

whyWrong.B: 18 comes from the discarded root -18 with its sign flipped; substituting 18 gives a surface area of \(1512\pi\).
whyWrong.C: 21 is the height, r + 6, not the radius.
whyWrong.D: 24 makes the surface area \(2\pi(576) + 2\pi(24)(30) = 2592\pi\), far too large.

questions.note: The book writes "right-angular cylinder" and "surface are"; transcribed as right circular cylinder and surface area.

questions.stem:
For data set \(A\), the table summarizes the distribution of the number of pieces of mail received by a business each day during a period of 11 days.
Pieces of mailDays
