questions.stem: A square map has a side length of 35 inches, and 1 inch on the map represents an actual distance of 17 miles. A smaller version of the same map is printed as a square with the side length 55% shorter than the side length of the previous map. On the smaller map, which of the following is closest to the actual distance, in miles, represented by 1 inch?
questions.whyCorrect: The map shrinks but the land it shows does not, so each inch has to stand for more miles. The real side represented is \(35 \times 17 = 595\) miles. "55% shorter" means the new side is \(45\%\) of 35, that is \(15.75\) inches. So 1 inch now represents \(\frac{595}{15.75} \approx 37.78\) miles.

whyWrong.A: This is \(17 \times 0.45\) — shrinking the scale along with the paper. Shrinking the paper makes each inch cover more ground, not less.
whyWrong.B: This is \(17 \times 0.645\) or similar; it again scales the miles-per-inch downward.
whyWrong.C: This is \(17 \times 1.13\), roughly, and would follow from taking the new side as 55% of the old rather than 45%, and then shrinking instead of stretching.

questions.stem: The function g is defined as \[ g(x) = \frac{2x - 4}{(x + 11)(x - 6)} \]If g(a + 5) = 0, where a is a constant, what is the value of a?
questions.whyCorrect: A fraction equals 0 exactly when its numerator is 0 and its denominator is not. So set the numerator to 0 at the input a + 5: 2(a + 5) - 4 = 0, giving 2a + 6 = 0 and a = -3. Check the denominator at the input a + 5 = 2: (13)(-4) is not 0, so the value is genuinely 0.

questions.stem: If \(\frac{x}{y} = 76\) and \(\frac{cx}{4y} = 76\), what is the value of \(c\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Write the second equation as \(\frac{c}{4} \cdot \frac{x}{y} = 76\). Substituting \(\frac{x}{y} = 76\) gives \(\frac{c}{4} \cdot 76 = 76\), so \(\frac{c}{4} = 1\) and \(c = 4\). Both expressions equal the same number, so the extra factor \(\frac{c}{4}\) must be 1.

questions.stem: \[ x^{2} - 12x + c = 0 \] In the given equation, c is a constant. The equation has no real solutions if \( c > n \) . What is the least possible value of n?
questions.whyCorrect: No real solutions means a negative discriminant: \( (-12)^{2} - 4c < 0 \) , so \( 144 < 4c \) and \( c > 36 \) . The condition in the stem is \( c > n \) , so the smallest n that still forces no real solutions is exactly 36.

whyWrong.A: -36 has the sign of the inequality backwards; every c below 36 gives a positive discriminant and two real solutions.
whyWrong.B: -12 is the coefficient b copied out of the equation rather than a bound on c.
whyWrong.C: 12 comes from \( \frac{144}{12} \) or from using b instead of \( b^{2} \) . Try c = 20: the discriminant is \( 144 - 80 = 64 \) , which is positive, so real solutions still exist.

questions.stem: If \(4 + \frac{5(3-x)}{2} = \frac{8(3-x)}{3}\) , what is the value of \(3 - x\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Do not expand the parentheses — treat \(3 - x\) as a single unknown, say \(u\). The equation becomes \(4 + \frac{5u}{2} = \frac{8u}{3}\). Multiply every term by 6 to clear the denominators: \(24 + 15u = 16u\), so \(u = 24\).

questions.stem: \[ 7x^{2}(4x-13)(4x-u) = 0 \]In the given equation, u is a positive constant. The sum of the solutions to the equation is 9. What is the value of u ?
questions.whyCorrect: Set each factor to zero: \( x^{2}=0 \) gives x = 0, \( 4x-13=0 \) gives \( x = \frac{13}{4} \) , and \( 4x-u=0 \) gives \( x = \frac{u}{4} \) . The distinct solutions sum to \( 0 + \frac{13}{4} + \frac{u}{4} = 9 \) , so \( \frac{u}{4} = 5.75 \) and u = 23. Zero counts once in the sum even though \( x^{2} \) is a repeated factor.
questions.note: The book prints "the sum of the the solutions to the equations"; the doubled word and the plural have been corrected.

questions.stem: Which system of linear equations has no solution?
questions.whyCorrect: For no solution the coefficients must be proportional while the constants are not. In D, multiply −5x + 9y = 8 by −2: the left side becomes 10x − 18y, exactly matching the second equation, but the right side becomes −16 while the second equation says 16. Proportional coefficients with a mismatched constant means parallel distinct lines.

whyWrong.A: Multiplying the first equation by −1 turns it into 5x − 9y = 8, which is the second equation. The constant scales along with everything else, so this is one line and there are infinitely many solutions.
whyWrong.B: \(\frac{5}{6} \ne \frac{-9}{10}\), so the coefficients are not proportional at all. The lines have different slopes and meet at exactly one point.
whyWrong.C: Scaling the first equation by −3 gives −15x − 27y = −24, but the second equation has +27y. The signs on the y-terms do not match, so these are not parallel lines — they cross once.

questions.stem: Anton is selling toys from his toy collection. When he started selling the toys, there were 2,800 toys in the collection. At the end of each week after Anton started selling the toys, the number of toys in the collection had decreased by \( \frac{1}{2} \) of the toys in the collection at the end of the previous week. Which equation gives the number of toys, c, in the collection w weeks after Anton started selling the toys, where \( 0 \le w \le 36 \)?
questions.whyCorrect: Losing half of what is left each week means the remaining amount is multiplied by \( \frac{1}{2} \) each week, so the model is exponential decay: starting amount times \( \left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^{w} \). The starting amount is the count before any weeks pass, which is 2,800, and it belongs in front as the coefficient.

whyWrong.A: This has no starting amount at all — at w = 0 it gives 0 toys, not 2,800 — and it is a square root, not a repeated halving.
whyWrong.B: Putting w in the exponent of 2,800 makes the collection grow enormously. The number being repeatedly multiplied is the decay factor \( \frac{1}{2} \), not 2,800.
whyWrong.C: 1,400 is the number left after one week, not the number at the start. This model gives 1,400 at w = 0, which contradicts the stem.

questions.note: Book prints "At the end of each week for 3 weeks" while also giving the domain 0 <= w <= 36; the two are inconsistent. Transcribed without "for 3 weeks", which does not affect the answer.

questions.stem:
\(x^2+y=21\)
−x + y = 1

The solutions to the given system of equations are of the form \((x,y)\). What is a possible value of \(x\) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Solve the linear equation for \(y\): \(y=x+1\). Substituting into the first equation gives \(x^2+x+1=21\), so \(x^2+x-20=0\) and \((x+5)(x-4)=0\). The solutions are \(x=-5\) and \(x=4\); only \(-5\) is offered.

whyWrong.B: \(-4\) is the other root with its sign flipped; the second solution is \(+4\), not \(-4\).
whyWrong.C: \(-1\) comes from the linear equation's constant, not from solving the system.
whyWrong.D: 21 is the constant in the first equation. Substituting it gives \(441+22\ne 21\).

questions.stem: \[ f = \frac{(10x)^{2}}{7g} \]The given equation relates the positive numbers \( f \), \( x \), and \( g \). Which equation correctly expresses \( x \) in terms of \( f \) and \( g \)?
questions.whyCorrect: Multiply both sides by \( 7g \) to get \( 7fg = (10x)^{2} = 100x^{2} \). Then \( x^{2} = \frac{7fg}{100} \), and taking the positive square root gives \( x = \frac{\sqrt{7fg}}{10} \). The 10 is inside the square, so it comes out as 10, not \( \sqrt{10} \).

whyWrong.B: This multiplies by 10 instead of dividing — it undoes \( \frac{x}{10} \) rather than \( 10x \).
whyWrong.C: This square-roots the 10 along with everything else, but \( (10x)^{2} = 100x^{2} \), so the divisor under the root would have to be 100.
whyWrong.D: Subtracting 10 undoes addition, not multiplication; nothing in the equation adds 10.

questions.stem: Eli used wax to make candles. The function f(x) = −15x + 60 approximates the weight, in ounces, of wax Eli had remaining after making x candles. Which statement is the best interpretation of the y-intercept of the graph of y = f(x) in the xy-plane in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: Eli had approximately 15 ounces of wax when he began to make the candles.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Eli used approximately 15 ounces of wax for each candle.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Eli had approximately 60 ounces of wax when he began to make the candles.

choices.label: D
choices.content: Eli used approximately 60 ounces of wax for each candle.

questions.whyCorrect: The y-intercept is f(0) = 60, the wax remaining after making zero candles — in other words, what he started with. Read the question carefully: it asks about the intercept, so the answer must be about 60, and it must describe a starting amount rather than a rate.

whyWrong.A: 60 is the intercept, not 15. The 15 is the slope.
whyWrong.B: This is a correct reading of the slope, but the question asks about the y-intercept.
whyWrong.D: This attaches the intercept value to a per-candle rate. The amount used per candle is 15 ounces; 60 is the total he began with.

questions.stem: \[ p(v) = 15v \]The function p gives the relationship between the instantaneous power p(v), in watts, and the potential difference v, in volts, for a current of 150 amperes. Which statement is the best interpretation of p(3) = 450 in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: For a potential difference of 3 volts, the instantaneous power is 450 watts.

choices.label: B
choices.content: For a current of 3 amperes, the instantaneous power is 450 watts.

choices.label: C
choices.content: For an instantaneous power of 3 watts, the potential difference is 450 volts.

choices.label: D
choices.content: For a current of 150 amperes, the potential difference is 450 volts.

questions.whyCorrect: Match each number to the role it plays in the notation. The 3 is the input v, which the stem defines as the potential difference in volts; the 450 is the output p(v), the instantaneous power in watts. So 3 volts produces 450 watts. The 150 amperes is a fixed condition of the whole model, not either coordinate.

whyWrong.B: The input v is a potential difference in volts, not a current in amperes. The current is fixed at 150 throughout.
whyWrong.C: This swaps input and output. The 3 goes in and the 450 comes out, not the other way round.
whyWrong.D: 450 is the output of p, so it is measured in watts, not volts. This choice also reports no information the notation p(3) = 450 actually carries.

questions.stem: A car travels at a speed of at least 25 miles per hour but no more than 50 miles per hour for a certain part of a trip. Which inequality represents this situation, where x is the speed of the car, in miles per hour, on this part of the trip?
questions.whyCorrect: "At least 25" gives a lower bound and "no more than 50" gives an upper bound, so both are needed and both endpoints are included.

whyWrong.A: The lower bound alone allows a speed of 200 miles per hour, which the stem rules out.
whyWrong.B: This makes 50 a minimum when the stem makes it a maximum.
whyWrong.D: 75 is 25 + 50, a sum with no meaning here, and this allows speeds below 25.

questions.stem: Circle \(N\) has a radius of 8 millimeters (mm). Circle \(M\) has an area of \(144\pi\) mm<sup>2</sup>. What is the total area, in mm<sup>2</sup>, of circles \(N\) and \(M\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Circle \(N\)'s area is \(\pi r^{2} = \pi(8)^{2} = 64\pi\). Adding circle \(M\)'s \(144\pi\) gives \(64\pi + 144\pi = 208\pi\) square millimeters.

whyWrong.A: \(20\pi\) adds the radius 8 to something like a radius of 12 — it combines lengths, not areas.
whyWrong.B: \(160\pi\) uses \(16\pi\) (the circumference of circle \(N\)) instead of its area \(64\pi\).
whyWrong.C: \(176\pi\) uses \(32\pi\) for circle \(N\), doubling the radius rather than squaring it.

questions.stem: If 350% of \(n\) is 35, what is the value of \(n\)?
questions.whyCorrect: 350% means 3.5, so the equation is \(3.5n = 35\) and \(n = 10\). Because the percent is above 100, \(n\) has to be smaller than 35 — that alone eliminates the three large choices.

whyWrong.A: 12,250 is 350 × 35; you multiplied instead of dividing and never converted the percent to a decimal.
whyWrong.B: 1,225 is \(35^{2}\), which no step of this problem produces.
whyWrong.C: 1,000 comes from mishandling the \(\div 100\) in the percent conversion, dividing 35 by 0.035 instead of 3.5.

questions.stem: \[ f(x) = (x - 4)^{2} + 11 \] What is the minimum value of the given function?
questions.whyCorrect: The squared term cannot be negative, so the smallest \( f(x) \) gets is when \( (x - 4)^{2} = 0 \) , at x = 4. That leaves 11, the minimum value.

whyWrong.A: 4 is the input at which the minimum occurs, not the output.
whyWrong.B: 7 subtracts 4 from 11. The 4 lives inside the square and never combines with the 11.
whyWrong.D: 15 adds them, for the same reason. At x = 4 the squared term contributes 0.

questions.stem: An arborist measured and recorded the heights of red maple trees in a certain area. Of the red maple tree heights recorded in this area, the minimum was 42 feet and the maximum was 57 feet. Which inequality is true for all possible values of t, where t represents the recorded height, in feet, of a red maple tree in this area?
questions.whyCorrect: A minimum is the smallest recorded value and a maximum the largest, so every height lies between them inclusive. Both bounds are needed, which is what the double inequality expresses.

whyWrong.A: 42 is the smallest height, so heights are at least 42, not at most 42.
whyWrong.B: 57 is the largest height, so heights are at most 57, not at least 57.
whyWrong.C: 99 is 42 + 57, a sum with no meaning here. No recorded tree was that tall.

questions.stem:
A farmer gave two groups of chickens different types of chicken feed for a month to measure the effect on egg production. The lists give the number of eggs collected from each chicken in each of the two groups.
Group G: 8, 16, 18, 18, 24
Group H: 16, 18, 18, 24
Which statement correctly compares the median number of eggs collected for group G and the median number of eggs collected for group H?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The median number of eggs collected for group G is equal to the median number of eggs collected for group H.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The median number of eggs collected for group G is greater than the median number of eggs collected for group H.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The median number of eggs collected for group G is less than the median number of eggs collected for group H.

choices.label: D
choices.content: There is not enough information to compare the median number of eggs collected for group G and the median number of eggs collected for group H.

questions.whyCorrect: Group G has 5 values, so its median is the middle one: 18. Group H has 4 values, so its median is the average of the two middle ones, \( \frac{18 + 18}{2} = 18 \). They are the same. The extra low value of 8 in G drags the mean down but leaves the median untouched.

whyWrong.B: Adding 8 to the bottom of group H produces group G, which pulls the mean down and cannot pull the median up. Both medians are 18.
whyWrong.C: The 8 does lower the mean of G, but the median of G is still the middle value 18, equal to H.
whyWrong.D: Both lists are given in full, so both medians can be computed exactly. Nothing is missing.

questions.stem: The width of a rectangle is 7 centimeters. The length of the rectangle is 40 centimeters longer than the width. What is the area, in square centimeters, of this rectangle?
questions.whyCorrect: "40 longer than the width" means length = 7 + 40 = 47, not 40. Then the area is 47 × 7 = 329 square centimeters.

whyWrong.A: 7 is the width by itself.
whyWrong.B: 14 is twice the width; no multiplication by the length has happened.
whyWrong.C: 54 is 7 + 47, the length plus the width (half the perimeter), not their product.

questions.stem: What is the y-intercept of the graph of \( y = 6^{x} + 12 \) in the xy-plane?
questions.whyCorrect: The y-intercept is the value at x = 0. Since \( 6^{0} = 1 \), not 0 and not 6, you get \( y = 1 + 12 = 13 \), so the point is (0, 13).

whyWrong.A: 6 is the base, not the value of \( 6^{0} \). Anything nonzero to the power 0 is 1.
whyWrong.B: 12 comes from treating \( 6^{0} \) as 0, which is the mistake this question is built around.
whyWrong.C: 18 comes from treating \( 6^{0} \) as 6 and adding it to 12.

questions.stem: A survey was conducted in Arlington to estimate the percent of adult residents who support the addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in their town. Based on the survey, it is estimated that 51% of all adult residents of Arlington support the addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in their town, with an associated margin of error of 7%. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about all adult residents of Arlington?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in the town is supported by more than 58% of all adult residents of Arlington.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Arlington who support the addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in their town are between 44% and 58%.

choices.label: C
choices.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Arlington who support the addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in their town are either less than 44% or more than 58%.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The addition of a gas station at a popular intersection in the town is supported by exactly 44% of all adult residents of Arlington.

questions.whyCorrect: A margin of error turns a single estimate into an interval of plausible values for the whole population: the estimate plus or minus the margin. Here that is 51% − 7% to 51% + 7%, or 44% to 58%. The correct conclusion states that interval and calls the values inside it plausible - it does not claim a single exact figure or rule out the estimate.

whyWrong.A: 58% is the top of the interval, not a floor. The survey supports values as low as 44%, so it cannot say support exceeds 58%.
whyWrong.C: This has the interval inside out. The plausible values are the ones inside 44% to 58%, not outside it.
whyWrong.D: A margin of error exists precisely because the exact population percentage is unknown. Naming one exact value, and the endpoint of the interval at that, contradicts the whole idea.

questions.stem: The perimeter of an equilateral triangle is 876 centimeters. The three vertices of the triangle lie on a circle. The radius of the circle is \( w\sqrt{3} \) centimeters. What is the value of w?
questions.whyCorrect: The side is \( \frac{876}{3} = 292 \) . For an equilateral triangle the circumradius is \( R = \frac{s}{\sqrt{3}} \) (from \( R = \frac{s}{2\sin 60^{\circ}} \) ), so \( R = \frac{292}{\sqrt{3}} = \frac{292\sqrt{3}}{3} \) . Matching that against \( w\sqrt{3} \) gives \( w = \frac{292}{3} \) . Do not confuse this with the inradius \( \frac{s}{2\sqrt{3}} \) , which is half as large.
questions.note: Exact value 292/3, about 97.33. Enter as the fraction 292/3.

questions.stem: The value of a painting increased by 186% from the end of 2011 to the end of 2012 and then decreased by 21% from the end of 2012 to the end of 2013. What was the net percentage increase in the value of the painting from the end of 2011 to the end of 2013?
questions.whyCorrect: Turn each change into a multiplier: up 186% gives \(1 + 1.86 = 2.86\), down 21% gives \(1 - 0.21 = 0.79\). Multiplying, \(2.86 \times 0.79 = 2.2594\), so the painting ends at 225.94% of its 2011 value, a net increase of 125.94%.

whyWrong.B: \(1.86 \times 0.79 = 1.4694\): this uses 1.86 as the multiplier, which drops the original value out of the 2012 figure.
whyWrong.C: \(186 - 21 = 165\). Successive percent changes multiply; subtracting the percentages ignores that the 21% comes off a much larger amount.
whyWrong.D: \(2.86 \times 1.21 = 3.46\), reported as a 246% increase — the second change was applied as a rise instead of a fall.

questions.stem:
For the right circular cone shown, B is a point on the circumference of the base, and the length of segment AB (not shown) is 84 centimeters. If the height of the cone is 42 centimeters and the volume of the cone is \( k\pi \) cubic centimeters, what is the value of k?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.whyCorrect: AB runs from the apex to a point on the base circle, so it is the slant height, and slant height, height and radius form a right triangle. That gives \( r^{2} = 84^{2} - 42^{2} = 7056 - 1764 = 5292 \) — and notice you never need r itself, only \( r^{2} \) . Then \( V = \frac{1}{3}\pi r^{2}h = \frac{1}{3}\pi(5292)(42) = 74{,}088\pi \) , so k = 74,088.
questions.note: Measured reading of the figure: a right circular cone standing point-up, apex labelled A, with a dashed vertical segment from A to the centre of the base marking the height, and B marked as a point on the base circle at the left.
questions.imageAlt: Line drawing of a right circular cone standing point up, with the apex labelled A, a dashed segment from the apex to the centre of the circular base, and a marked point B on the base circle.

questions.stem: The area of a rectangular region is increasing at a rate of 210 square feet per hour. Which of the following is closest to this rate in square meters per minute? (Use 1 meter = 3.28 feet.)
questions.whyCorrect: Two conversions are needed and the area one is squared. Since 1 m = 3.28 ft, 1 m² = \(3.28^2 = 10.7584\) ft², so \(210 \div 10.7584 \approx 19.52\) square meters per hour. Dividing by 60 minutes gives about 0.33 square meters per minute.

whyWrong.B: This divides by 3.28 once instead of squaring it: \(\frac{210}{60} \div 3.28 \approx 1.07\). Converting an area needs the conversion factor twice, once for each dimension.
whyWrong.C: \(\frac{210}{60} \times 3.28 \approx 11.48\) — multiplying where you should divide. A square meter is larger than a square foot, so the number of square meters must come out smaller.
whyWrong.D: 19.52 is the correct rate in square meters per hour; the conversion to minutes was never done.

questions.stem: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the acute angles is \( (7x-610)^\circ \). The sum of the measures of one of the acute angles and three of the obtuse angles is \( (-14x+w)^\circ \). What is the value of \(w\)?
questions.whyCorrect: With two parallel lines and a transversal, all four acute angles are equal and each obtuse angle is the supplement of an acute one. Writing the acute measure as \( a = 7x-610 \), the required sum is \( a+3(180-a) = 540-2a \). Substituting, \( 540-2(7x-610) = 540-14x+1220 = -14x+1760 \), so matching the given form gives \( w = 1760 \).

questions.stem: The graph below shows the distribution of all stars within 12 light-years of Earth by total energy output per second, or luminosity. Which of the following could be the median luminosity of all the stars within 12 light-years of Earth?
questions.whyCorrect: Add the bars: \(9 + 7 + 5 + 6 + 3 + 1 = 31\) stars, so the median is the 16th star counting from the dimmest. The dimmest band (below 0.001) holds 9 stars, taking positions 1 through 9, and the next band (0.001 to 0.01) holds 7, taking positions 10 through 16. The 16th star therefore lies in the 0.001-to-0.01 band, and only 0.0063 falls in it.

whyWrong.A: 0.18 sits in the 0.1-to-1 band, which covers positions 22 through 27 — well past the middle.
whyWrong.B: 0.052 sits in the 0.01-to-0.1 band, positions 17 through 21. It is one band too bright.
whyWrong.D: 0.0003 is below 0.001, in the dimmest band, which only reaches position 9.

questions.note: The graph is not printed with this question; it appears with the identical question 48 on PDF page 84 as a horizontal bar chart titled "Luminosity of Stars within 12 Light-Years", number of stars per luminosity band: greater than 10: 1; 1 to 10: 3; 0.1 to 1: 6; 0.01 to 0.1: 5; 0.001 to 0.01: 7; less than 0.001: 9. | figure: The graph is not printed beside this question in the book; it is reproduced from the identical question 48 on page 84, where the same chart appears.
questions.imageAlt: Horizontal bar chart titled Luminosity of Stars within 12 Light-Years; the horizontal axis at the top gives the number of stars and each bar is a luminosity band.

questions.stem: In triangle \(FGH\) and triangle \(KLM\), the measures of angles \(G\) and \(L\) are each 60°. The lengths of \(GH\) and \(LM\) are each 34 centimeters, and \[ \frac{GH}{GF} = \frac{LM}{LK} \]Which additional piece of information would be necessary to prove that triangle \(FGH\) is congruent to triangle \(KLM\):

choices.label: A
choices.content: The lengths of \(FG\) and \(KM\) are each 17 centimeters.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The measures of angles \(H\) and \(M\) are each 30°.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The measures of angles \(F\) and \(K\) are each 90°.

questions.whyCorrect: The proportion already does the work. Since \( GH = LM = 34 \), the equation \( \frac{GH}{GF} = \frac{LM}{LK} \) forces \( GF = LK \). So the two triangles have \( GH = LM \), \( GF = LK \), and the angle between those two sides equal (\( G = L = 60^\circ \)) — that is SAS, which already proves congruence.

whyWrong.A: Pinning \(FG\) to 17 adds nothing that is not already implied, and it pairs \(FG\) with \(KM\), which is not the side corresponding to \(FG\) (that is \(KL\)).
whyWrong.B: An extra angle is unnecessary once SAS is satisfied, and there is no reason these angles must be 30°.
whyWrong.C: Same problem: the congruence is already established, and nothing forces \(F\) and \(K\) to be right angles.

questions.stem: For which of the following sets of 9 data points is the median less than the mean?
questions.whyCorrect: Median below mean means the data are pulled to the right by a few high values, so look for the plot with its bulk on the left and a tail stretching right. Set A has four dots at 1, two at 2 and one each at 3, 4 and 5: the fifth value in order is 2, while the mean is \(\frac{4(1)+2(2)+3+4+5}{9}=\frac{20}{9}\approx 2.22\). Median 2 is less than mean 2.22. In set B the median is 4 against a mean of about 3.44, in set C the plot is symmetric so median and mean are both 3, and in set D the median is 4 against a mean of about 3.78 - all three have the median at or above the mean.

whyWrong.B: Set B is left-skewed (1, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, 4, 5, 5): median 4, mean \(\frac{31}{9}\approx 3.44\), so the median is greater than the mean.
whyWrong.C: Set C (1, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3, 4, 4, 5) is symmetric about 3, so the median equals the mean rather than falling below it.
whyWrong.D: Set D (1, 2, 3, 4, 4, 5, 5, 5, 5) is left-skewed: median 4, mean \(\frac{34}{9}\approx 3.78\).

questions.stem: In triangle RST, the measure of angle R is 18 degrees and the measure of angle T is 72 degrees. Point L lies on \( \overline{RS} \) , point K lies on \( \overline{ST} \) , and \( \overline{LK} \) is parallel to \( \overline{RT} \) . What is the measure, in degrees, of angle SKL? (Disregard the degree symbol when entering your answer.)
questions.whyCorrect: You do not need angle S at all. \( \overline{ST} \) crosses the two parallel segments \( \overline{LK} \) and \( \overline{RT} \) , so angle SKL at K and angle STR at T are corresponding angles and are equal. Angle STR is angle T, which is 72°. (The 18° at R is there to tempt you into solving for angle S = 90° first, which is not needed.)
questions.note: Same template as Hard Book Geometry #5, with the angles given as numbers rather than expressions. Do not place both in one test.

questions.stem:
For 100 neurons, the table summarizes the distribution of classification and cell body diameter.
ClassificationCell body diameter (micrometers)
Less than 2020 to 30Greater than 30
Sensory neuron1230
Motor neuron01718
Interneuron10320
One of these neurons will be selected at random. What is the probability of selecting a neuron with a cell body diameter that is less than or equal to 30 micrometers, given that it is not classified as a motor neuron? (Express your answer as a decimal or fraction, not as a percent.)
questions.whyCorrect: A conditional probability restricts the pool first. Dropping the motor neurons leaves the sensory neurons (12 + 3 + 0 = 15) and the interneurons (10 + 32 + 0 = 42), for 57 neurons. Both of those rows have 0 in the "greater than 30" column, so every one of the 57 has a diameter of 30 micrometers or less: the probability is \(\frac{57}{57} = 1\).
questions.note: DEFECT, two of them: the table entries sum to 92, not the 100 neurons the stem claims, and the conditional probability comes out to exactly 1 because neither non-motor row has any neuron above 30 micrometers. Needs repair before use.

questions.stem: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of these eight angles is \( (7x - 250)^{\circ} \) . The sum of the measures of four of the eight angles is \( k^{\circ} \) . Which of the following could NOT be equivalent to k, for all values of x?
questions.whyCorrect: A transversal across two parallel lines makes only two distinct measures: four copies of an acute angle a and four of its supplement 180 - a. Take a = 7x - 250, so the obtuse measure is 430 - 7x. Any four of the eight angles sum to one of five values: 4a = 28x - 1,000; 3a + one obtuse = 14x - 320; two and two = 360; one acute and three obtuse = 1,040 - 14x; four obtuse = 1,720 - 28x. (Starting from the obtuse angle instead produces the same five.) Choices B, C and D are on that list; \( -14x + 1{,}540 \) is not — the matching entry is \( -14x + 1{,}040 \) .

whyWrong.B: 14x - 320 is the sum of three acute angles and one obtuse: 3(7x - 250) + (430 - 7x).
whyWrong.C: -28x + 1,720 is the sum of all four obtuse angles: 4(430 - 7x).
whyWrong.D: 360 is the sum of two acute and two obtuse angles, since each acute-obtuse pair adds to 180. It is a valid sum for every x.

questions.stem:
Data set A: 8, 11, 12, 15, 21, 27
Data set B: 9, 12, 13, 16, 22, \(h\)

Data sets \(A\) and \(B\) each consist of 6 values as shown, where \(h\) is a constant. If the standard deviation of data set \(A\) is greater than the standard deviation of data set \(B\), which of the following could be the value of \(h\)?

I. 23
II. 28
III. 29
questions.whyCorrect: Compare B with A term by term: 9, 12, 13, 16, 22 are exactly 8, 11, 12, 15, 21 each increased by 1. So if \(h = 28\), data set B is data set A shifted up by 1, and shifting every value by the same amount leaves the standard deviation unchanged — equal, not greater, so II fails. Making \(h\) larger than 28 stretches B's spread further, so III fails too. Only \(h = 23\) pulls the last value in toward the rest, making B's spread smaller than A's.

whyWrong.B: \(h = 28\) makes B a copy of A shifted up 1 unit. A shift moves the mean but not the spread, so the two standard deviations are equal and A's is not greater.
whyWrong.C: \(h = 29\) puts the top value even further from B's mean than 27 is from A's, so B's standard deviation comes out larger than A's, the opposite of what is required.
whyWrong.D: Both of these values make B at least as spread out as A, so neither satisfies the condition.

questions.stem: In isosceles triangle ABC, sides AB and AC are congruent. Point D divides side BC such that the length of BD is \(\frac{4}{7}\) of the length of BC. Point E lies on side AB and point F lies on side AC such that when segments DE and DF are drawn, angle BED is congruent to angle CFD. If the length of BE is 8, what is the length of CF?
questions.whyCorrect: Because AB and AC are congruent, the base angles satisfy angle B = angle C. You are also told angle BED = angle CFD. Two pairs of congruent angles give triangle BED ~ triangle CFD, with B matching C, E matching F and D matching D. Since BD is \(\frac{4}{7}\) of BC, CD is \(\frac{3}{7}\) of BC, so the ratio of similarity is BD : CD = 4 : 3. Then BE : CF = 4 : 3, and CF = 8 × \(\frac{3}{4}\) = 6.

whyWrong.B: This comes from adding rather than scaling — 8 + 6, or treating the 4 : 3 split as something to add onto the given length. The similar triangles give a multiplicative relationship, not an additive one.
whyWrong.C: This is 8 × 4, using the numerator of \(\frac{4}{7}\) as the scale factor. The scale factor is BD : CD = 4 : 3, not 4 : 1, and it must shrink BE, not enlarge it.
whyWrong.D: This is 8 × 7, using the whole of BC against BD. The triangle containing CF sits on CD, which is \(\frac{3}{7}\) of BC, not on BC itself.

questions.stem:
\[ g(x) = \frac{2}{7}x + \frac{8}{5} \]
\[ h(x) = 5x - 7 \] The functions g and h are defined by the equations shown. Which expression is equivalent to \( g(x) \cdot h(x) \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Multiply all four pairs. \( \frac{2}{7}x \cdot 5x = \frac{10x^{2}}{7} \) , \( \frac{2}{7}x \cdot (-7) = -2x \) , \( \frac{8}{5} \cdot 5x = 8x \) , and \( \frac{8}{5} \cdot (-7) = -\frac{56}{5} \) . The two middle terms combine to \( -2x + 8x = 6x \) , which is positive.

whyWrong.A: This drops the two cross terms. They do not cancel: -2x and 8x leave 6x.
whyWrong.B: \( \frac{13x}{6} \) comes from adding the numbers in the two fractions instead of multiplying the terms out. Both cross terms are whole multiples of x.
whyWrong.C: The sign on the middle term is wrong. \( \frac{8}{5} \cdot 5x = 8x \) is larger than \( \frac{2}{7}x \cdot (-7) = -2x \) , so the sum is +6x.

questions.stem: \[ P = N(34 - C) \]The given equation relates the variables \( P \), \( N \), and \( C \). Which expression represents the value of \( C \) for distinct positive values of \( P \) and \( N \)?
questions.whyCorrect: Divide both sides by \( N \) first, which keeps the parentheses intact: \( \frac{P}{N} = 34 - C \). Then move \( C \) across and \( \frac{P}{N} \) across to get \( C = 34 - \frac{P}{N} \). Dividing before expanding is what makes this one line of work.

whyWrong.A: An expression for \( C \) cannot contain \( C \) itself, so this has not isolated anything.
whyWrong.B: The sign is wrong: \( \frac{P}{N} = 34 - C \) rearranges to \( C = 34 - \frac{P}{N} \), not \( 34 + \frac{P}{N} \).
whyWrong.C: This divides by \( C \) instead of \( N \), and it leaves \( C \) on both sides.

questions.note: Same template as expressions-61 (44 replaced by 34, and the left side there is PC rather than P); the two are close enough to flag at allocation.

questions.stem:
\[ w^2+8w-28=0 \]
Which of the following is a solution to the given equation?
questions.whyCorrect: The quadratic formula gives \(w=\frac{-8\pm\sqrt{64+112}}{2}=\frac{-8\pm\sqrt{176}}{2}\). Simplify the radical before dividing: \(\sqrt{176}=4\sqrt{11}\), so \(w=\frac{-8\pm 4\sqrt{11}}{2}=-4\pm 2\sqrt{11}\).

whyWrong.A: The sign of the \(-4\) is wrong. Since \(b=8\), \(-b=-8\), and dividing by 2 gives \(-4\).
whyWrong.B: This keeps only the radical part and drops the \(-4\); both terms in the numerator have to be divided by 2 and kept.
whyWrong.C: \(\sqrt{11}\) drops the \(-4\) and also mis-simplifies \(\frac{\sqrt{176}}{2}\), which is \(2\sqrt{11}\).

questions.stem: If \(\frac{x-18}{30} = \frac{x-18}{6}\) , what is the value of \(x + 18\)?
questions.whyCorrect: The same quantity \(x - 18\) sits on top of both fractions, and the denominators are different, so the only way the two sides can be equal is if that quantity is zero. Cross-multiplying gives \(6(x-18) = 30(x-18)\), so \(24(x-18) = 0\) and \(x = 18\). The question asks for \(x + 18 = 36\).

whyWrong.A: This is the value of \(x - 18\), not \(x + 18\). Read the last line again.
whyWrong.B: There is no step that produces 5; it comes from misreading the denominators as something to subtract.
whyWrong.C: This is \(x\) itself. The question asks for \(x + 18\).

questions.stem: A researcher observes a sample of a nuclide. An exponential model estimates that the mass, in grams, of the sample decreases by 23% every 21.87 minutes. Which of the following equations could represent this model, where M is the estimated mass, in grams, of the sample t minutes after the researcher began observing the sample?
questions.whyCorrect: Decreasing by 23% leaves 77% behind, so the multiplier is 0.77, not 0.23. That multiplier applies once every 21.87 minutes, so over t minutes it applies \( \frac{t}{21.87} \) times — a repeated event goes in the exponent as a division by the length of one period.

whyWrong.B: 0.23 is the fraction lost, not the fraction remaining. Using it would leave only 23% of the mass after one period instead of 77%.
whyWrong.C: Wrong on both counts: 0.23 is the fraction lost, and adding 21.87 to the exponent shifts the model rather than setting the period length. At t = 0 this gives far less than the starting mass.
whyWrong.D: The multiplier 0.77 is right, but t + 21.87 in the exponent means the decay has already been running for 21.87 minutes at t = 0, which contradicts the starting mass.

questions.stem:
\(y = -\frac{1}{3}x\)
\(y = \frac{1}{5}x\)

The solution to the given system of equations is \((x, y)\). What is the value of \(x\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Both lines go through the origin and their slopes differ, so they cross only there. Setting them equal, \(-\frac{1}{3}x = \frac{1}{5}x\) gives \(-5x = 3x\), so \(8x = 0\) and \(x = 0\).

whyWrong.A: \(-3\) is a denominator from the first equation; substituting it gives \(y = 1\) on one line and \(y = -0.6\) on the other, so it is not a common point.
whyWrong.C: 2 does not appear in either equation and is not a solution.
whyWrong.D: 5 is the other denominator, and it fails the same check: the two lines give different \(y\) values there.

questions.stem:
\[ y = -4x^{2} - 23 \]
\[ y = qx - 19 \] In the given system of equations, q is a positive constant. The graphs of the equations in the given system intersect at exactly one point (x, y) in the xy-plane. What is the value of x?
questions.whyCorrect: Set the two expressions for y equal: \( -4x^{2} - 23 = qx - 19 \) rearranges to \( 4x^{2} + qx + 4 = 0 \) . One intersection point means one solution, so the discriminant is zero: \( q^{2} = 4(4)(4) = 64 \) and q = 8 because q is positive. A quadratic with one solution has that solution at its vertex, \( x = -\frac{q}{2(4)} = -1 \) .

whyWrong.A: -42 is -(23 + 19), which adds the two constants instead of moving one across the equals sign. It is not an x-value.
whyWrong.B: -27 combines constants from the two equations directly rather than solving for where the graphs meet.
whyWrong.C: -8 is \( -q \) , which skips the division by \( 2a = 8 \) in the vertex formula.

questions.stem: The function f(x) = −30x + 310 gives the predicted height above the ground f(x), in feet, of a model airplane x minutes after it begins to descend. What is the predicted height above the ground, in feet, of the model airplane 2 minutes after it begins to descend?
questions.whyCorrect: Minutes are the input, so substitute 2 for x: f(2) = −30(2) + 310 = −60 + 310 = 250. The 310 is the starting height and 30 feet is lost each minute, so after 2 minutes the plane has dropped 60 feet.

whyWrong.A: 60 is the distance the plane descends in 2 minutes, not the height it has reached.
whyWrong.C: 280 subtracts only one minute's descent, treating x = 1 instead of x = 2.
whyWrong.D: 370 adds 60 to 310 instead of subtracting, ignoring the negative slope.

questions.note: The book's stem names the variable 'a minutes after it begins to descend' while the function is written in x; transcribed as x for consistency.

questions.stem:
Two data sets each containing 20 integers are summarized in the table. Each row gives the frequency of integers greater than or equal to the first bound and less than the second.
IntegerFrequency in Data Set AFrequency in Data Set B
30 to less than 4008
40 to less than 5044
50 to less than 6085
60 to less than 7083
The mean of Data Set A is equal to a. The mean of Data Set B is equal to b. What is the smallest possible value of \(\frac{b}{a}\)?
questions.whyCorrect: A fraction is smallest when its numerator is as small as possible and its denominator as large as possible, so make b minimal and a maximal. For b, put every integer at the bottom of its interval: 8(30) + 4(40) + 5(50) + 3(60) = 830, so \(b_{\min}=\frac{830}{20}=41.5\). For a, push every integer to the top of its interval - and because the intervals exclude their upper bound and the values are integers, the largest allowed are 49, 59 and 69, not 50, 60 and 70. That gives 4(49) + 8(59) + 8(69) = 1,220, so \(a_{\max}=\frac{1220}{20}=61\). The smallest ratio is \(\frac{41.5}{61}=\frac{83}{122}\approx 0.680\).
questions.note: The book prints two histograms with bin width 10 over 30 to 70; bar heights sit on gridlines, so the equivalent frequency table is exact. Two things about the printed stem: its description of the intervals is garbled (it says the first interval is 40 to 50 and the second is 30 to 40, running backwards), and the exact answer 83/122 = 0.6803... is not a tidy grid-in value; on a real test it would be entered as .680. Worth a human check.

questions.stem: In the figure, \( AC = CD \). The measure of angle \(EBC\) is 29°, and the measure of angle \(ACD\) is 108°. What is the value of \(x\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Triangle \(ACD\) is isosceles with \( AC = CD \), so its base angles are equal: \( \frac{180-108}{2} = 36^\circ \) each, which makes angle \(CDA\) — and therefore angle \(BDE\), since \(C\) lies on \( \overline{DB} \) — equal to 36°. Now look at triangle \(DBE\): the angle at \(D\) is 36° and the angle at \(B\) is 29° (angle \(EBC\) is the same as angle \(EBD\)). The angle \(x^\circ\) is exterior to that triangle at \(E\), so it equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: \( 36+29 = 65 \).
questions.note: Figure needed: D, E, A collinear left to right; C above between D and B; segment DB through C; segment CA; segment BE meeting DA at E; x is the angle at E between EB and EA.
questions.imageAlt: A plane diagram with a horizontal base line carrying three labelled points, a slanted line from the left-hand end rising to a labelled point above, and two further segments drawn across the interior; one angle is marked with a letter.

questions.stem: A real estate company offers a series of three webinars. 1,250 people attended the first webinar. 68% of the people who attended the first webinar attended the second webinar, and 32% of the people who attended the first and second webinars attended the third webinar. How many people attended all three webinars?
questions.whyCorrect: Each percentage is taken of the group named just before it, not of the original 1,250. First to second: 0.68(1,250) = 850 people attended both the first and second. The 32% is then applied to that group of 850, not to 1,250: 0.32(850) = 272. The trap is multiplying 1,250 by 32% (which gives 400) or by 68% + 32% = 100%.

questions.stem: A line intersects two parallel lines, forming four acute angles and four obtuse angles. The measure of one of the acute angles is (9x − 490)°. The sum of the measures of one of the acute angles and three of the obtuse angles is (−18x + w)°. What is the value of w?
questions.whyCorrect: When a transversal cuts two parallel lines, every acute angle is congruent to every other acute angle and every obtuse angle is supplementary to them. So each obtuse angle measures 180 − (9x − 490). One acute plus three obtuse is (9x − 490) + 3[180 − (9x − 490)] = 540 − 2(9x − 490) = 540 − 18x + 980 = 1520 − 18x. Matching that to −18x + w gives w = 1520. Notice you never need x itself — the −18x on both sides is the signal that the x-terms are meant to cancel.

questions.stem:
The table shows the distribution of the ages \(x\), in years, of the 21 stamps in Ari's original collection, where \(y\) is the number of stamps of each age.
\(x\)\(y\)
856
905
9510
Total21
Ari will add a 135-year-old stamp to her original collection, creating a new collection of 22 stamps. Which statement correctly compares the mean ages and median ages of Ari's original and new collections?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The mean age for the new collection is greater than the mean age for the original collection, and the median age for the new collection is greater than the median age for the original collection.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The mean age for the new collection is greater than the mean age for the original collection, but the median age is the same for the original and new collections.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The mean age for the new collection is less than the mean age for the original collection, and the median age for the new collection is less than the median age for the original collection.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The median age for the new collection is greater than the median age for the original collection, but the mean age is the same for the original and new collections.

questions.whyCorrect: The new stamp is older than every stamp already there, so the mean rises: 1,910 ÷ 21 ≈ 90.95 becomes 2,045 ÷ 22 ≈ 92.95. The median rises too, and that is the part worth checking rather than assuming. With 21 stamps the median is the 11th, and positions 7–11 are all 90, so the original median is 90. With 22 stamps it is the average of the 11th and 12th; position 12 is the first of the ten 95s, so the new median is (90 + 95) ÷ 2 = 92.5.

whyWrong.B: The median does move here. It only stays put when the values on either side of the new middle position are equal, and in this collection position 11 is 90 while position 12 is 95.
whyWrong.C: Adding a value larger than every existing one cannot lower either measure.
whyWrong.D: The mean cannot stay the same: the new stamp is 135 years old against an existing mean near 91, so it pulls the mean up.

questions.note: The book prints the table with bare headers x and y and no sentence saying what they represent; the lead-in identifying x as the age in years and y as the number of stamps has been restored so the question is answerable.

questions.stem:
In the figure shown, point T lies on segment SW, and segment TU is parallel to segment VW. The measure of angle V is 26°, and the measure of angle STU is 74°. What is the value of \( p - r \) ?

Note: Figure not drawn to scale.
questions.whyCorrect: Treat SW as a transversal of the parallel segments TU and VW: angle STU and the angle at W open the same way on the same side, so they are corresponding angles and r = 74. Then look at trapezoid TUVW: UV is a transversal of the same two parallel segments, so the angles at U and V are same-side interior angles and add to 180, giving p = 180 - 26 = 154. Therefore p - r = 154 - 74 = 80.
questions.note: Measured reading of the figure: S is at the top, W at the lower left with T on segment SW between them, U is to the right of T and V at the lower right, forming trapezoid TUVW with TU parallel to WV. The angle marked p is the interior angle at U, and r is the interior angle at W.
questions.imageAlt: Line drawing of trapezoid T U V W with S on the extension of side W T above T; the angle at U is labelled p degrees and the angle at W is labelled r degrees.

questions.stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, for the data set P. A line of best fit for the data is also shown. Data set Q is created by adding 540 units to the value of x for each data point from the data set P. Which of the following could be an equation of a line of best fit for the data set Q?
questions.whyCorrect: Sliding every point 540 units to the right shifts the line right by 540 but does not tilt it, so the slope is unchanged and only the constant moves. First get the slope from the graph: the drawn line climbs from about 14.2 at x = 100 to about 14.95 at x = 130, a rise of 0.75 over a run of 30, or about 0.027 — that is \( \frac{35}{1301} \), not \( \frac{1}{131} \approx 0.0076 \). Then apply the shift: replacing x by x - 540 lowers the constant by \( 540 \times \frac{35}{1301} \approx 14.5 \), and the original constant is about 14.2 - 100(0.027) ≈ 11.5, leaving about -3.

whyWrong.B: The slope \( \frac{1}{131} \) is about a third of the slope drawn on the graph, so this line is far too flat whatever its constant is.
whyWrong.C: Same wrong slope as choice B.
whyWrong.D: This has the right slope but the constant has been moved the wrong way. Shifting the data to larger x must decrease the value at x = 0, not raise it by about 14.5.

questions.note: Scatterplot, x from about 95 to 132 and y from 13 to 15.2, with a line of best fit from about (98, 14.2) to (130, 14.95). Points approximately (102, 14.4), (105, 14.6), (108, 14.5), (113, 14.6), (117, 14.8), (118, 14.7), (127, 14.9), (128, 15.0), (130, 15.05). The book prints the choices without a leading "y =". | figure: The page shows ten points; the recorded spec listed nine, omitting one near x = 129 and giving the rightmost point as 15.05 rather than 15.0. Drawn from the page.
questions.imageAlt: Scatterplot with x on the horizontal axis running from about 100 to 130 and y on the vertical axis from 13 to 15, showing ten plotted points and a straight line of best fit drawn through them.

questions.stem: The perimeter of an isosceles right triangle is \(52+52\sqrt{2}\) inches. What is the length, in inches, of the hypotenuse of this triangle?
questions.whyCorrect: An isosceles right triangle with leg \(a\) has hypotenuse \(a\sqrt{2}\), so its perimeter is \(2a+a\sqrt{2}=a(2+\sqrt{2})\). Set that equal to \(52+52\sqrt{2}=52(1+\sqrt{2})\) and solve: \(a=\frac{52(1+\sqrt{2})}{2+\sqrt{2}}\). Multiply top and bottom by \(2-\sqrt{2}\); the denominator becomes 2 and the numerator becomes \(52\sqrt{2}\), so \(a=26\sqrt{2}\). The hypotenuse is \(a\sqrt{2}=26\sqrt{2}\cdot\sqrt{2}=52\). The trap is that the perimeter is written to look like it splits as leg + leg + hypotenuse; it does not.

whyWrong.A: This is half of 52, which would be the answer if you read the perimeter's first term, 52, as the sum of the two legs. The two parts of \(52+52\sqrt{2}\) are not the legs and the hypotenuse.
whyWrong.B: This is the leg length \(a\), the value you get partway through. The question asks for the hypotenuse, which is \(a\sqrt{2}\).
whyWrong.D: This treats the \(52\sqrt{2}\) term of the perimeter as the hypotenuse directly. If it were, the two legs would sum to 52, making each leg 26 and the hypotenuse \(26\sqrt{2}\), which contradicts the assumption.

questions.stem:
The frequency table summarizes a data set of the weights, rounded to the nearest pound, of 71 Ardeotis kori birds.
Weight (pounds)Frequency
1312
