A weight of 32 pounds is added to the original data set, creating a new data set of the weights, rounded to the nearest pound, of 72 Ardeotis kori birds. Which statement best compares the mean and the median of the new data set to the mean and median of the original data set?

choices.label: A
choices.content: The mean of the new data set is greater than the mean of the original data set, and the median of the new data set is greater than the median of the original data set.

choices.label: B
choices.content: The mean of the new data set is greater than the mean of the original data set, and the medians of the two data sets are equal.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The mean of the new data set is less than the mean of the original data set, and the median of the new data set is less than the median of the original data set.

choices.label: D
choices.content: The mean of the new data set is less than the mean of the original data set, and the median of the new data set is greater than the median of the original data set.

questions.whyCorrect: 32 pounds is far above the original mean of about 16.65, so the mean rises, to 1,214 ÷ 72 ≈ 16.86. For the median, put the rows in weight order and build a running total: 13 reaches 12, 14 reaches 22, 15 reaches 25, 16 reaches 30, 17 reaches 37. With 71 birds the median is the 36th value, which falls in the 17-pound block. With 72 birds it is the average of the 36th and 37th, and both are still 17, so the median is unchanged.

whyWrong.A: The median does not move. One extra value at the top of 71 shifts the middle by half a position, and the 36th and 37th values are both 17.
whyWrong.C: Adding a weight far above the existing mean raises it; it cannot lower it.
whyWrong.D: Both halves are wrong: the mean rises rather than falls, and the median stays at 17.

questions.note: The book prints the weight rows out of order (13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19, 18, 20), kept as printed; and prints "data sat" for "data set", corrected.

questions.stem: The functions g and h are defined by the given equations. \[ g(x) = \sqrt{(x - 11)^{2} + 45} \] \[ h(x) = \sqrt[3]{64} + \frac{x^{2}}{2} \] If the value of \( g(8) = t \) , where t is a constant, what is the value of \( h(t) \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: You never need the decimal value of t. \( g(8) = \sqrt{(8 - 11)^{2} + 45} = \sqrt{9 + 45} = \sqrt{54} \) , so \( t^{2} = 54 \) , which is the only thing h asks for. Then \( h(t) = \sqrt[3]{64} + \frac{54}{2} = 4 + 27 = 31 \) .

whyWrong.A: \( 3\sqrt{6} \) is \( \sqrt{54} \) , which is t itself. The question asks for \( h(t) \) , so t still has to go into h.
whyWrong.B: 22 is \( 4 + 18 \) , which requires \( t^{2} = 36 \) . The radicand is \( 9 + 45 = 54 \) , not 36.
whyWrong.D: 51 is not produced by any correct step; it comes from squaring \( 3\sqrt{6} \) incorrectly or from adding 45 a second time. Check that \( t^{2} = 54 \) and that only half of it is added to 4.

questions.stem: A right rectangular prism has a base area of \(56t\) square centimeters (cm²). The length of the base of the rectangular prism is \(\frac{14}{3}\) cm, and the height of the rectangular prism is 3 cm. Which expression represents the surface area, in cm², of the right rectangular prism?
questions.whyCorrect: First get the base width: area ÷ length \(= 56t \div \frac{14}{3} = 56t \cdot \frac{3}{14} = 12t\). Surface area is two bases plus the side faces: \(2(56t) + (\text{base perimeter})(\text{height}) = 112t + 2\left(\frac{14}{3} + 12t\right)(3) = 112t + 28 + 72t = 184t + 28\).

whyWrong.A: This doubles the base area and then adds 56 instead of computing the four side faces from the perimeter.
whyWrong.C: 1,680 comes from multiplying rather than dividing when finding the width, inflating the side-face contribution.
whyWrong.D: This omits the constant term entirely, which comes from the two faces whose area is \(\frac{14}{3} \times 3\) each.

questions.stem: \[ f(x) = 14x^{2} - 35x + 7 \] The given equation defines the function f. For what value of x does \( f(x) \) reach its minimum?
questions.whyCorrect: The leading coefficient is positive, so the parabola opens upward and its minimum sits at the vertex. The vertex is at \( x = -\frac{b}{2a} = \frac{35}{2(14)} = \frac{35}{28} = 1.25 \) .

whyWrong.B: 1.75 is \( \frac{35}{20} \) , which uses the wrong denominator. The formula divides by \( 2a = 28 \) , not by 20.
whyWrong.C: 7 is the constant term, which is the value of \( f(0) \) , not the location of the vertex.
whyWrong.D: 35 is the coefficient b. It still has to be divided by \( 2a \) and given the opposite sign.

questions.stem: If \(\frac{x-4}{5} = \frac{x-4}{7}\) , the value of \(x - 4\) is between which of the following pairs of values?
questions.whyCorrect: Two fractions with the same numerator and different denominators can only be equal when that numerator is 0. Cross-multiplying gives \(7(x-4) = 5(x-4)\), so \(2(x-4) = 0\) and \(x - 4 = 0\). Zero lies between \(-3\) and 3.

whyWrong.A: Nothing in the equation produces a negative value near \(-6\); the denominators are not solutions.
whyWrong.C: This interval brackets 4, which is the value of \(x\) itself. The question asks where \(x - 4\) lies, and that is 0.
whyWrong.D: This interval brackets 5 to 7, the two denominators; those are not the value of \(x - 4\).

questions.stem: A researcher observes a sample of a nuclide. An exponential model estimates that the mass, in grams, of the sample decreases by 27% every 14.07 minutes. Which of the following equations could represent this model, where M is the estimated mass, in grams, of the sample t minutes after the researcher began observing the sample?
questions.whyCorrect: A 27% decrease leaves 73% of the mass, so the multiplier is 0.73. That multiplier applies once per 14.07-minute period, and the number of periods in t minutes is \( \frac{t}{14.07} \), which is what belongs in the exponent.

whyWrong.A: 0.27 is the fraction lost, not the fraction kept. This model would destroy 73% of the sample each period.
whyWrong.B: Both parts fail: 0.27 is the wrong multiplier, and t + 14.07 in the exponent shifts the starting point instead of scaling the period.
whyWrong.D: 0.73 is right, but adding 14.07 to t means the decay has already run for a full period at t = 0, so the model never gives the starting mass.

questions.note: Near-identical template to satmath-ma3-exponential-functions-11 (23% every 21.87 minutes); do not place both in one test.

questions.stem:
\(y = -\frac{1}{7}x\)
\(y = \frac{1}{11}x\)

The solution to the given system of equations is \((x, y)\). What is the value of \(x\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Both equations have no constant term, so both lines pass through the origin; with different slopes that is their only shared point. Algebraically: \(-\frac{1}{7}x = \frac{1}{11}x\) gives \(-11x = 7x\), so \(18x = 0\) and \(x = 0\).

whyWrong.A: \(-7\) is a denominator from the first equation; substituting gives \(y = 1\) on one line and \(y = -\frac{7}{11}\) on the other, so it is not a shared point.
whyWrong.C: 4 appears nowhere in the system and fails the same check.
whyWrong.D: 11 is the other denominator, and the two lines give different \(y\) values there.

questions.stem:
\[ y = 6x^{2} - 48x + 98 \]
\[ y + 4 = 0 \] How many solutions does the given system of equations have?
questions.whyCorrect: The second equation is just the horizontal line \( y = -4 \) , so substitute: \( 6x^{2} - 48x + 98 = -4 \) gives \( 6x^{2} - 48x + 102 = 0 \) , or \( x^{2} - 8x + 17 = 0 \) , whose discriminant is \( 64 - 68 = -4 \) . No real x works. Geometrically the parabola opens upward with its lowest point at (4, 2), which is above the line \( y = -4 \) , so they never meet.

whyWrong.A: Exactly one solution would mean the line is tangent at the vertex, which would require the line \( y = 2 \) .
whyWrong.B: Two solutions would need the line to cut through the parabola, so it would have to sit above y = 2. The line is at -4.
whyWrong.C: A parabola and a horizontal line can meet at most twice, so 3 is impossible for any values.

questions.stem: Which expression is equivalent to \(2(xy^{2} + x^{2}y) - 8(xy^{2} - 4x^{2}y)\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Distribute both coefficients, keeping the sign on the second: \(2xy^{2} + 2x^{2}y - 8xy^{2} + 32x^{2}y\). The \(-8\) times \(-4x^{2}y\) is \(+32x^{2}y\). Combining like terms gives \(-6xy^{2} + 34x^{2}y\).

whyWrong.B: \(33x^{2}y\) uses \(32 + 1\); the first bracket contributes \(2x^{2}y\), not \(x^{2}y\).
whyWrong.C: \(-30x^{2}y\) comes from distributing \(-8\) over \(-4x^{2}y\) as \(-32x^{2}y\); two negatives multiply to a positive.
whyWrong.D: Same sign error on the \(32x^{2}y\) term, combined with using \(1x^{2}y\) instead of \(2x^{2}y\) from the first bracket.

questions.stem: \[ g(x) = x^{3} + ax^{2} + bx + c \] The function g is defined by the given equation, where a, b, and c are integer constants. The zeros of the function are -2, -7, and 6. What is the value of a?
questions.whyCorrect: The zeros give the factored form \( g(x) = (x + 2)(x + 7)(x - 6) \) . Multiplying the first two gives \( x^{2} + 9x + 14 \) , and multiplying by \( (x - 6) \) gives an \( x^{2} \) term of \( -6x^{2} + 9x^{2} = 3x^{2} \) , so a = 3. The shortcut is that for a cubic with leading coefficient 1, a is the negative of the sum of the zeros: \( -(-2 - 7 + 6) = 3 \) .

whyWrong.A: -84 is the constant term c, which comes from multiplying the zeros: \( (2)(7)(-6) = -84 \) . It is not the \( x^{2} \) coefficient.
whyWrong.B: -3 is the sum of the zeros itself. The coefficient a is the negative of that sum.
whyWrong.D: 84 is the product of the zeros with the sign flipped, and it belongs to the constant term, not to \( x^{2} \) .

questions.stem: If \(12 + \frac{7(3-x)}{6} = \frac{5(3-x)}{3}\) , which equation must also be true?
questions.whyCorrect: Treat \(3 - x\) as a single unknown \(u\) instead of expanding: \(12 + \frac{7u}{6} = \frac{5u}{3}\). Multiply through by 6 to clear denominators: \(72 + 7u = 10u\), so \(3u = 72\) and \(u = 24\). That means \(3 - x = 24\), and negating both sides gives \(x - 3 = -24\).

whyWrong.A: 207 does not come from this equation at all; \(3u = 72\) gives 24.
whyWrong.B: You have the sign backwards. \(3 - x\) equals \(+24\), so it is \(x - 3\) that equals \(-24\).
whyWrong.C: Wrong value and wrong sign — neither 207 nor a positive right side follows from \(3u = 72\).

questions.stem: The function \(f\) is defined by \(f(x)=5x^2\). What is the value of \(f(6)\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Substitute 6 for \(x\) and square before you multiply. \(f(6)=5(6)^2=5\cdot 36=180\). The exponent applies only to \(x\), not to the 5.

whyWrong.A: You multiplied \(5\cdot 6\) and then added 6 — the squaring was dropped entirely.
whyWrong.B: This has no route from the function; it looks like a guess near \(5\cdot 6\).
whyWrong.C: You treated \(5x^2\) as \((5x)\cdot 2\), doubling instead of squaring: \(5\cdot 6\cdot 2=60\).

questions.stem: What is the slope of the graph of 48x − 6y = −32 in the xy-plane?
questions.whyCorrect: Rearrange into y = mx + b. Subtracting 48x gives −6y = −48x − 32, and dividing every term by −6 gives \( y = 8x + \frac{16}{3} \) . The slope is 8. Dividing by a negative number flips both signs on the right - miss that and you get the wrong sign.

whyWrong.A: −8 keeps the sign from −48x without accounting for dividing by −6.
whyWrong.B: \( -\frac{3}{2} \) is not the coefficient of x in slope-intercept form; it comes from combining the wrong pair of numbers.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{3}{2} \) has the same problem as B, just with the sign changed.

questions.stem: The function f is defined by \( f(x) = 2x^{3} + \frac{1}{3}x^{2} - x \) . What is the value of f(1)?
questions.whyCorrect: Every power of 1 equals 1, so the expression becomes \( 2 + \frac{1}{3} - 1 = \frac{4}{3} \) .

whyWrong.B: 2 keeps only the leading term.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{10}{3} \) adds the last term instead of subtracting it.
whyWrong.D: 6 comes from treating the coefficients as whole numbers and ignoring both the fraction and the subtraction.

questions.note: Duplicate of Functions & Function Notation #16 in the same book - identical stem and choices. Do not import both.

questions.stem:
Data set \(F\) consists of 55 integers, where the value of each integer is between 150 and 260. Data set \(G\) consists of the same 55 integers in \(F\) as well as the integer 10. Which of the following must be less for data set \(G\) than for data set \(F\)?

I. The mean
II. The median
questions.whyCorrect: The mean must fall, because 10 is below every value in \(F\) and so certainly below \(F\)'s mean; adding a value below the mean always pulls it down. The median need not fall. \(F\) has 55 values, so its median is the 28th; \(G\) has 56, so its median is the average of \(G\)'s 28th and 29th, which are \(F\)'s 27th and 28th. If \(F\)'s 27th and 28th values happen to be equal — nothing forbids it, since the integers may repeat — that average equals \(F\)'s median, so it is not less. "Must be less" fails for II.

whyWrong.B: The median is the one that can stay the same. The mean is the one that is forced down.
whyWrong.C: I is right but II is not guaranteed — repeated values around the middle position let the median stay exactly where it was.
whyWrong.D: The mean genuinely must decrease: 10 is far below every one of the 55 values, so it cannot leave the average unchanged or raise it.

questions.stem: A right square pyramid has a total surface area of 70,560 square inches, and the combined surface area of the four lateral faces of this pyramid is 38,160 square inches. What is the height, in inches, of this pyramid?
questions.whyCorrect: Peel it back one layer at a time. The base area is 70,560 - 38,160 = 32,400, so the base edge is \(\sqrt{32400} = 180\). The four triangular faces give \(4 \cdot \frac{1}{2}(180)\ell = 360\ell = 38{,}160\), so the slant height is \(\ell = 106\). Then the height, half the base edge (90), and the slant height form a right triangle: \(h = \sqrt{106^2 - 90^2} = \sqrt{3136} = 56\).

whyWrong.B: 90 is half the base edge — the horizontal leg of the right triangle, not the vertical height.
whyWrong.C: 106 is the slant height, measured up the sloping face rather than straight up the middle.
whyWrong.D: 180 is the base edge.

questions.stem: The positive number \(a\) is 2,352% of the sum of the positive numbers \(b\) and \(c\), and \(b\) is 84% of \(c\). What percent of \(b\) is \(a\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Everything has to end up in terms of \(b\). From \(b = 0.84c\) you get \(c = \frac{b}{0.84}\), so \(b + c = b\left(1 + \frac{1}{0.84}\right) = \frac{46}{21}b\). Then \(a = 23.52(b + c) = 23.52 \cdot \frac{46}{21}b = 51.52b\). Finally convert back to a percent: \(a\) is 51.52 times \(b\), which is 5,152%.

whyWrong.B: This comes from adding the two percents (2,352 + 84) instead of chaining them through the sum \(b + c\).
whyWrong.C: 51.52 is the correct multiplier, but the question asks for a percent, so it must be multiplied by 100. \(a\) is over fifty times \(b\), not half of it.
whyWrong.D: This both mishandles the chain and leaves the answer as a decimal multiplier read as a percent.

questions.stem: \[ |x - 8| = -|x - 8| + 20 \]What is the sum of the solutions to the given equation?
questions.whyCorrect: Treat \( |x - 8| \) as one quantity and collect it: adding \( |x - 8| \) to both sides gives \( 2|x - 8| = 20 \) , so \( |x - 8| = 10 \) . An absolute value of 10 means x - 8 = 10 or x - 8 = -10, so x = 18 or x = -2, and the sum is 16. (A shortcut: the two solutions are symmetric about x = 8, so their sum is 2 · 8 = 16.)
Do not solve for \(x\) and \(y\). Recognise \(x^{6} - y^{6}\) as a difference of squares of \(x^{3}\) and \(y^{3}\): \(x^{6} - y^{6} = (x^{3} + y^{3})(x^{3} - y^{3}) = 12 \times 6 = 72\).

questions.stem: Function \(f\) is a quadratic function. The graph of \(y = f(x)\) in the xy-plane has a vertex at \((4, -6)\), contains the point \((3, 8)\), and has a y-intercept at \((0, a)\). The graph of \(y = 5 + f(x)\) has a y-intercept at \((0, b)\). What is the positive difference between \(a\) and \(b\)?
questions.whyCorrect: You never need the vertex or the point. Adding 5 to a function shifts its whole graph up 5 units, so \(b = 5 + f(0)\) while \(a = f(0)\); the difference is 5 no matter what \(f\) is. If you do want to check: the vertex gives \(f(x) = c(x - 4)^2 - 6\), and \(f(3) = 8\) forces \(c = 14\), so \(a = f(0) = 218\) and \(b = 223\), a difference of 5.

questions.stem: The cost to rent a bus from Company X is $950 for the first 2 hours and an additional $50 per hour for each hour after the first 2 hours. If the total cost to rent the bus from Company X for \( t \) hours, where \( t > 2 \), is $1,250, which equation represents this situation?
questions.whyCorrect: The $950 is charged once and already pays for the first 2 hours, so it is a constant, not a rate. The hours billed at $50 are the ones past the second, and there are \( t - 2 \) of them, giving 950 + 50(t − 2) = 1,250.

whyWrong.A: This multiplies the one-time $950 by the number of extra hours and then charges $50 for every hour as well.
whyWrong.B: Both terms are wrong: the flat fee is scaled by \( 2t \), and all \( t \) hours are charged the hourly rate.
whyWrong.D: \( 2t \) doubles the total time instead of removing the first 2 hours, so the extra hours are miscounted.

questions.note: Same template as linear-equations-9 (3 hours there, 2 here); flag as a near-duplicate pair at allocation.

questions.stem: One of the factors of \( 4x^{3} + 88x^{2} + 468x \) is \( x + b \) , where b is a positive constant. What is the smallest possible value of b ?
questions.whyCorrect: Factor out \( 4x \) first: \( 4x(x^{2} + 22x + 117) \) . Then find two numbers with product 117 and sum 22 — they are 9 and 13 — so the expression is \( 4x(x+9)(x+13) \) . The two factors of the form \( x + b \) give b = 9 and b = 13, and the smaller is 9.
questions.note: Near-duplicate of #22 in this chapter, which is the same polynomial scaled by 2 instead of 4 and has the same answer.

questions.stem: A scientist makes batches of bricks using different sand-to-cement ratios to test how the sand-to-cement ratio affects the strength of the brick. For one batch of bricks, the scientist uses 4,880 cubic centimeters (cm³) of sand and cement, where the ratio of the volume of sand to the volume of cement is 7 to 3. If \(s\) represents the volume, in cm³, of sand and \(c\) represents the volume, in cm³, of cement that the scientist uses for this batch of bricks, which system of equations represents this situation?
questions.whyCorrect: The 4,880 is the combined volume, so the total equation is \(s + c = 4{,}880\) — the 7 and 3 do not belong there. The ratio \(\frac{s}{c} = \frac{7}{3}\) cross-multiplies to \(3s = 7c\); note the numbers swap sides, which is the step most people get backwards.

whyWrong.A: \(s = c\) says equal volumes, contradicting the 7-to-3 ratio, and \(7s + 3c\) is not the total volume.
whyWrong.B: Same problem with \(s = c\), and the weighted sum again misrepresents the 4,880.
whyWrong.C: \(7s = 3c\) is the ratio inverted — it makes cement the larger volume, when sand should be.

questions.stem: The function f is defined by \( f(x) = a^{x} + b \), where a and b are constants and a > 0. In the xy-plane, the graph of \( y = f(x) \) has a y-intercept at (0, -22) and passes through the point (2, 41). What is the value of a + b?
questions.whyCorrect: Use the y-intercept first, because \( a^{0} = 1 \) regardless of a: \( f(0) = 1 + b = -22 \), so b = -23. Now put the second point in: \( a^{2} - 23 = 41 \), so \( a^{2} = 64 \) and, since a > 0, a = 8. Then a + b = 8 - 23 = -15.

questions.stem:
\(y = 5(x - 3)\)
\(y = (x - 3)^2\)
Which ordered pair \((x, y)\) is a solution to the given system of equations?
questions.whyCorrect: Set the two expressions for y equal: \((x-3)^2 = 5(x-3)\). Move everything to one side and factor out the common \((x-3)\): \((x-3)(x-8) = 0\), so \(x = 3\) or \(x = 8\). At \(x = 8\), \(y = 5(5) = 25\), giving \((8, 25)\). (The other solution is \((3,0)\), which is not offered.)

whyWrong.A: The x-value is right but the y-value is not: \(5(8-3) = 25\), not \(-5\).
whyWrong.C: At \(x = 3\) both equations give \(y = 0\), so the solution there is \((3,0)\), not \((3,8)\).
whyWrong.D: This satisfies the first equation only: \(5(2-3) = -5\), but \((2-3)^2 = 1\). A solution must satisfy both.

questions.stem: \[ 11m = 7(n + p) \]The given equation relates the positive numbers \( m \), \( n \), and \( p \). Which equation correctly gives \( n \) in terms of \( m \) and \( p \)?
questions.whyCorrect: Divide both sides by 7 before touching the parentheses: \( \frac{11m}{7} = n + p \). Then subtract \( p \): \( n = \frac{11m}{7} - p \). Expanding to \( 11m = 7n + 7p \) works too and gives the same result.

whyWrong.A: This has no \( m \) in the numerator and no \( p \) subtraction; it does not follow from either valid route.
whyWrong.C: This multiplies by 7 instead of dividing, and adds \( p \) instead of subtracting it — both operations go the wrong way.
whyWrong.D: This subtracts 7 rather than dividing by it. The 7 multiplies the whole parenthesis, so only division removes it.

questions.stem: The graph of the linear function f is shown, where y = f(x). The line slants gradually up from left to right and passes through the points \( (-6, -8) \) , \( (0, -7) \) and \( (6, -6) \) . What is the slope of the graph of f?
questions.whyCorrect: Slope is rise over run between any two points on the line. From \( (0, -7) \) to \( (6, -6) \) the y-value rises by 1 while x runs 6, so the slope is \( \frac{1}{6} \) . The line rises from left to right, so the slope has to be positive, and it rises slowly, so it has to be small.

whyWrong.B: −7 is the y-intercept of the line, not its slope.
whyWrong.C: \( -\frac{1}{6} \) has the right size but the wrong sign; a line that goes up from left to right has a positive slope.
whyWrong.D: 7 inverts the rise-over-run ratio and drops the sign of the intercept it was taken from.

questions.note: The book prints a graph but also lists the three points in text, so the question is answerable without the image.

questions.stem: The function g is defined by \[ g(x) = \sqrt{6x + 7}. \] What is the value of \( g(3) \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Work inside the radical first: \( 6(3) + 7 = 25 \) . Then take the square root: \( \sqrt{25} = 5 \) .

whyWrong.A: This divides the answer by 6, as if the 6 were a denominator. It multiplies the input instead.
whyWrong.B: This is 25 divided by 6 — the same misplacement of the 6, with the square root also skipped.
whyWrong.D: This is the value inside the radical. The square root still has to be taken.

questions.stem: A pet service that takes care of both cats and dogs can care for at most 43 animals. Which inequality represents this situation, where \(c\) is the number of cats and \(d\) is the number of dogs?
questions.whyCorrect: The total number of animals is cats plus dogs, \(c+d\). “At most 43” caps that total, so \(c+d\le 43\).

whyWrong.A: Subtracting counts the difference between the two groups, not the total.
whyWrong.B: Same subtraction error, plus a direction that would force a large surplus of cats.
whyWrong.C: \(\ge\) makes 43 a minimum; the service cannot exceed its capacity.

questions.stem: A cylinder has a diameter of 14 inches and a height of 8 inches. What is the volume, in cubic inches, of the cylinder?
questions.whyCorrect: The volume of a cylinder is \(V = \pi r^{2}h\), and the problem gives the diameter, not the radius. Halve 14 to get \(r = 7\), then \(V = \pi \cdot 7^{2} \cdot 8 = 392\pi\) cubic inches.

whyWrong.A: \(49\pi\) is the area of the circular base alone; you still have to multiply by the height.
whyWrong.B: \(112\pi\) is \(14 \times 8\pi\) — the diameter times the height, with no squaring of a radius at all.
whyWrong.D: \(1{,}568\pi = \pi \cdot 14^{2} \cdot 8\), which uses the diameter as the radius. That makes the volume four times too large.

questions.stem: In a random sample of 276 residents in a certain building, 9 residents reported that they take the train to work. If there are a total of 1,380 residents in this building, which of the following is the best estimate of the number of building residents who take the train to work?
questions.whyCorrect: Scale the sample up to the building. The building has \(\frac{1{,}380}{276}=5\) times as many residents as the sample, so multiply the 9 train riders by 5 to get 45. As a proportion: \(\frac{9}{276}=\frac{n}{1{,}380}\).

whyWrong.A: 9 is the count in the 276-person sample. The building is five times larger, so the estimate must be larger too.
whyWrong.C: 276 is the sample size, not a count of train riders.
whyWrong.D: 1,095 is \(1{,}380-285\)-style arithmetic; it would mean about 79% of residents take the train, when the sample rate is only about 3%.

questions.stem:
\[ f(x)=-8x^2+101x \]
The function \(f\) models the depth below sea level, in meters, of a certain seal \(x\) minutes after the seal dives into the water. What is the best interpretation of \(f(2)=170\) in this context?

choices.label: A
choices.content: 2 minutes after the seal dives into the water, its estimated depth is 170 meters below the sea level.

choices.label: B
choices.content: Approximately 2 minutes after the diving into the water, the sea level returns to sea level.

choices.label: C
choices.content: The sea level reaches an estimated maximum depth of 170 meters below sea level.

choices.label: D
choices.content: 170 minutes after the seal dives into the water, its estimated depth is 2 meters below the sea level.

questions.whyCorrect: The input \(x\) is time in minutes and the output \(f(x)\) is depth in meters, so \(f(2)=170\) reads directly as: at \(x=2\) minutes, the depth is 170 meters. Nothing needs to be computed — you only have to keep straight which quantity is the input and which is the output.

whyWrong.B: Returning to the surface would be \(f(x)=0\), not \(f(x)=170\); this also confuses the seal with the sea level.
whyWrong.C: A maximum would require the vertex, which is at \(x=\frac{101}{16}\approx 6.3\) minutes, not \(x=2\); the maximum depth is about 319 meters.
whyWrong.D: The 2 and the 170 are swapped. The number inside the parentheses is the time, and the value the function equals is the depth.

questions.stem: In the xy-plane, what is the slope of the line that passes through the points (0, 0) and (13, 14)?
questions.whyCorrect: Slope is the change in y divided by the change in x: \( \frac{14 - 0}{13 - 0} = \frac{14}{13} \) . The y-difference goes on top.

whyWrong.A: 13 is the run alone.
whyWrong.C: \( \frac{13}{14} \) is the reciprocal - it puts the change in x on top.
whyWrong.D: 14 is the rise alone.

questions.stem: A right circular cylinder has a height of 4 meters (m) and a base with a radius of 18 m. What is the volume, in \(\text{m}^3\), of the cylinder?
questions.whyCorrect: Volume of a cylinder is \(\pi r^2 h\). Square the radius before multiplying by the height: \(\pi(18)^2(4) = \pi(324)(4) = 1296\pi\).

whyWrong.A: This is the height alone; the base area is missing.
whyWrong.B: This adds 18 and 4 instead of using \(\pi r^2 h\).
whyWrong.C: This swaps the radius and the height: \(\pi(4)^2(18) = 288\pi\). The radius is the number that gets squared.

questions.stem: If 380% of \(n\) is 38, what is the value of \(n\)?
questions.whyCorrect: 380% is the multiplier 3.8, so the sentence is \(3.8n = 38\), giving \(n = 10\). Since 380% is more than 100%, the result 38 is bigger than \(n\), so \(n\) must be smaller than 38 — that rules out the three large choices immediately.

whyWrong.A: This is \(38 \times 380\), multiplying instead of dividing and skipping the conversion from percent.
whyWrong.B: This is \(38 \times 38\); the percent was never converted to a decimal.
whyWrong.C: This comes from dividing by 0.038 rather than 3.8 — the decimal moved two places too far.

questions.stem: The function f is defined by \( f(x) = a(4)^{x} \) , where a is a positive constant. In the xy-plane, the graph of y = f(x) passes through the point (0, 13). What is the value of f(0)?
questions.whyCorrect: Saying the graph passes through (0, 13) is the same as saying f(0) = 13 - the y-coordinate of a point on the graph is the function's output there. No computation with a is needed, though it also follows from \( f(0) = a(4)^{0} = a \) , so a = 13.

whyWrong.A: 4 is the base of the exponential, not an output.
whyWrong.B: 1 is \( 4^{0} \) , the exponential factor at x = 0, without the coefficient a.
whyWrong.D: 9 comes from 13 − 4, mixing the coefficient and the base.

questions.stem: The positive number \(a\) is 2,047% of the sum of the positive numbers \(b\) and \(c\), and \(b\) is 89% of \(c\). What percent of \(b\) is \(a\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Get \(b + c\) in terms of \(b\) alone. From \(b = 0.89c\), \(c = \frac{b}{0.89}\), so \(b + c = b\left(1 + \frac{100}{89}\right) = \frac{189}{89}b\). Then \(a = 20.47 \cdot \frac{189}{89}b = 43.47b\). Converting the multiplier to a percent, \(a\) is 4,347% of \(b\).

whyWrong.A: This is roughly \(\frac{1}{43.47}\) as a percent — the comparison made in the wrong direction, giving what percent of \(a\) is \(b\).
whyWrong.B: This mixes the 89% into the chain as a multiplier rather than solving \(c = \frac{b}{0.89}\).
whyWrong.C: This roughly adds 2,047% and the 89% relationship instead of chaining them, and never converts \(b + c\) into \(b\).

questions.note: Same template as this book's #33 with different numbers — do not place both in one test.

questions.stem: Triangles PQR and LMN are graphed in the xy-plane. Triangle PQR has vertices P, Q, and R at (5, 2), (5, 4), and (7, 2), respectively. Triangle LMN has vertices L, M, and N at (5, 2), \( (5,\ 4+k) \) , and \( (7+k,\ 2) \) , respectively, where k is a positive constant. If the measure of \( \angle Q \) is \( t^{\circ} \) , what is the measure of \( \angle N \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Both triangles have a right angle at the shared vertex (5, 2), because one leg is vertical and the other horizontal. In LMN the vertical leg is \( 4 + k - 2 = k + 2 \) and the horizontal leg is \( 7 + k - 5 = k + 2 \) — equal, so LMN is an isosceles right triangle and \( \angle N = 45^{\circ} \) . The same is true of PQR, so t = 45, and \( 90 - t = 45 \) . Choice C gives the right value; the k never enters because it lengthens both legs equally.

whyWrong.A: \( 90 - (t - k) = 45 + k \) , which grows with k. Stretching both legs by the same amount does not change the angles.
whyWrong.B: \( 90 - (t + k) = 45 - k \) , which shrinks with k and would go negative for k > 45.
whyWrong.D: \( 90 + k \) exceeds 90°, but N is an acute angle of a right triangle.

questions.stem: The scatterplot shows the relationship between two variables, x and y, for data set A. A line of best fit for the data is also shown. Data set B is created by subtracting 9 units from the value of y for each data point from data set A. Which of the following is closest to the y-coordinate of the y-intercept of the line of best fit for data set B?
questions.whyCorrect: Lowering every y-value by 9 slides the whole line down 9 units without tilting it, so the new intercept is the old intercept minus 9. Get the old one by extending the drawn line back to the y-axis: it passes through roughly (12, 45) and (37, 20), a slope of about -1, so at x = 0 it is near 57 — and the only choice 9 below a value in that region is 45.57. The trap is that the line starts well to the right of the y-axis, so the intercept has to be extrapolated, not read.

whyWrong.B: 53 would require the original line to cross at 62, which is above the top of the plotted y-axis and far above where the drawn line is heading.
whyWrong.C: 59.62 is roughly the original intercept region, so this is the answer you get by forgetting to subtract the 9.
whyWrong.D: 62.75 is higher still, and would need a much steeper line than the one drawn.

questions.note: Scatterplot, x from 0 to about 50 and y from 0 to 60, with a line of best fit through about (12, 45) and (37, 20). Points approximately (12, 45), (13, 45), (15, 42), (16, 41), (17, 39), (22, 32), (25, 30), (28, 24), (29, 31), (30, 25), (33, 30), (36, 20). A least-squares fit to those readings gives intercept 56 and slope -0.97, so the shifted intercept is about 47, nearest to choice A. | figure: The recorded spec's point coordinates were slightly off; the points were re-measured off the page and drawn from those readings.
questions.imageAlt: Scatterplot with x on the horizontal axis marked to 45 and y on the vertical axis marked to 60, showing twelve plotted points and a straight line of best fit drawn through them; the line does not reach the vertical axis.

questions.stem: A cube has an edge length of 82 inches. A solid sphere with a radius of 41 inches is inside the cube, such that the sphere touches the center of each face of the cube. To the nearest cubic inch, what is the volume of the space in the cube not taken up by the sphere?
questions.whyCorrect: The leftover space is the cube's volume minus the sphere's volume. The cube gives \(82^3 = 551{,}368\) and the sphere gives \(\frac{4}{3}\pi(41)^3 \approx 288{,}695.61\). Subtracting, \(551{,}368 - 288{,}695.61 \approx 262{,}672\).

whyWrong.B: This is the volume the sphere itself occupies, not the space left over around it.
whyWrong.C: This subtracts \(\pi r^3\) instead of \(\frac{4}{3}\pi r^3\); dropping the \(\frac{4}{3}\) makes the sphere too small and the leftover space too big.
whyWrong.D: This subtracts the area of a circle, \(\pi(41)^2 \approx 5{,}281\), instead of the volume of a sphere.

questions.stem: An object's speed is increasing at a rate of 3.9 meters per second squared. What is this rate, in miles per minute squared, rounded to the nearest tenth? (Use 1 mile = 1,609 meters.)
questions.whyCorrect: Convert the distance and the time separately, and remember the time unit is squared. Miles: divide by 1,609. Minutes: one minute is 60 seconds, and seconds appear squared in the denominator, so multiply by \(60^2 = 3600\). That gives \(\frac{3.9 \times 3600}{1609} \approx 8.73\), which rounds to 8.7.

whyWrong.A: This is \(\frac{3.9 \times 60}{1609}\) — the seconds converted once instead of squared.
whyWrong.C: This is \(\frac{3.9 \times 1609}{60}\): multiplying by 1,609 instead of dividing, and dividing by 60 instead of multiplying by 3,600.
whyWrong.D: Far too large for a distance in miles; no correct or near-correct combination of 1,609 and 60 produces it. The correct value is under 10.

questions.note: This book repeats this metres-per-second-squared to miles-per-minute-squared item several times (#6, #11, #13, #14, #16) with only the number changed — place at most one per test.

questions.stem: In triangle PQR, the measure of angle P is \((3x + 5)^\circ\), the measure of angle Q is \((2x + 9)^\circ\), and the measure of angle R is \((4y + 5)^\circ\). If side QR is extended through point R to point S and the measure of angle PRS is \((x + y)^\circ\), what is the value of \(x + y\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Angle PRS is the exterior angle at R, so it equals the sum of the two remote interior angles: \(x + y = (3x+5) + (2x+9) = 5x + 14\). It is also supplementary to angle R, so \((x+y) + (4y+5) = 180\). The first equation gives \(y = 4x + 14\); substituting into \(x + 5y = 175\) gives \(21x = 105\), so \(x = 5\) and \(y = 34\), and \(x + y = 39\). (Check: the angles are 20°, 19° and 141°, which sum to 180°.)

questions.stem: A number \(f\) is 120% greater than a positive number \(g\). A number \(h\) is 90% less than the number \(f\). The number \(h\) is how many times the number \(g\)?
questions.whyCorrect: "120% greater than" means you add 120% to the original, so \(f = g(1 + 1.20) = 2.2g\) — not \(1.2g\). "90% less than" means 90% is removed, leaving 10%: \(h = 0.10f\). Combining, \(h = 0.10(2.2g) = 0.22g\).

whyWrong.A: This uses \(f = 1.2g\), reading '120% greater than' as '120% of'. The word 'greater' adds the increase on top of the original.
whyWrong.C: This is \(1.2 \times 0.9\), using 90% as the fraction kept rather than the fraction removed.
whyWrong.D: This is \(2.2 \times 0.9\) — the first step right, but keeping 90% instead of the 10% that is left after a 90% reduction.

questions.stem: The line segment shown in the xy-plane represents one of the legs of a right triangle. The area of this triangle is \(48\sqrt{13}\) square units. What is the length, in units, of the other leg of this triangle?
questions.whyCorrect: First get the length of the drawn leg from its endpoints with the distance formula: the horizontal change is 9 and the vertical change is 6, so the length is \(\sqrt{9^{2}+6^{2}}=\sqrt{117}=3\sqrt{13}\). For a right triangle the two legs are the base and the height, so \(\frac{1}{2}(3\sqrt{13})(L)=48\sqrt{13}\). Multiply by 2 and divide by \(3\sqrt{13}\): \(L=\frac{96\sqrt{13}}{3\sqrt{13}}=32\). The \(\sqrt{13}\) cancels entirely, which is the sign you set it up correctly.

whyWrong.A: This is what you get if you write the area as (leg)(leg) instead of \(\frac{1}{2}\)(leg)(leg) — it is exactly half of the right answer.
whyWrong.C: This is the length of the leg already drawn, not the other one.
whyWrong.D: This doubles the drawn leg. Doubling is not what the area equation asks for; you have to divide the doubled area by the drawn leg, and the radical cancels when you do.

questions.note: Figure needed: a line segment in the xy-plane from (-5, 3) to (4, 9), drawn on a grid with x from -8 to 8 and y from 0 to 16.
questions.imageAlt: A line segment with both endpoints marked, drawn on a square grid in the xy-plane; the x-axis runs from -8 to 8 and the y-axis from 0 to 16.

questions.stem: A raised garden is in the shape of a right rectangular prism. Its base has a width of 3 feet and a length of 27 feet, and it will be filled 24 inches high with topsoil. The total cost of the topsoil needed to fill the garden to this height is 234 dollars. What is the unit cost, in dollars per cubic yard, for the topsoil? (1 yard = 3 feet; 1 foot = 12 inches)
questions.whyCorrect: Put all three dimensions in feet: 24 inches is 2 feet, so the volume is \(3 \times 27 \times 2 = 162\) cubic feet. Converting volume cubes the length factor — one cubic yard is \(3^3 = 27\) cubic feet — so the volume is \(\frac{162}{27} = 6\) cubic yards. The unit cost is \(\frac{234}{6} = 39\) dollars per cubic yard.
questions.note: Identical to this book's Unit Conversion #7 apart from the total cost (234 vs 198) — do not place both in one test.

questions.stem: A right circular cone has a volume of \(2{,}700\pi\) cubic centimeters and the area of its base is \(225\pi\) square centimeters. What is the slant height, in centimeters, of this cone?
questions.whyCorrect: The base area gives the radius: \(\pi r^{2}=225\pi\), so \(r=15\). Now use \(V=\frac{1}{3}(\text{base area})h\): \(\frac{1}{3}(225\pi)h=2{,}700\pi\), so \(75h=2{,}700\) and \(h=36\). The slant height is the hypotenuse of the right triangle formed by the radius and the height: \(\sqrt{15^{2}+36^{2}}=\sqrt{1{,}521}=39\). The last step is the one students skip — slant height is not the height.

whyWrong.A: This is \(2{,}700\div225\), which drops the \(\frac{1}{3}\) from the cone volume formula. Including it gives a height of 36, not 12.
whyWrong.B: This is the radius, an intermediate value.
whyWrong.C: This is the vertical height of the cone. The slant height runs along the surface from the apex to the edge of the base, so it is the hypotenuse of the triangle with legs 15 and 36 and is longer than 36.

questions.stem: A researcher surveyed undergraduate students, graduate students, and postdoctoral students. The number of undergraduate students surveyed was 7,150% of the number of postdoctoral students surveyed and the number of graduate students surveyed was 45% of the number of undergraduate students surveyed. If there were 6,435 graduate students surveyed, what was the sum of the number of undergraduate students and postdoctoral students surveyed?
questions.whyCorrect: Work backwards from the number you are given. Graduates are 45% of undergraduates: \(0.45U = 6{,}435\), so \(U = 14{,}300\). Undergraduates are 7,150% of postdoctoral students, i.e. \(U = 71.5P\), so \(P = \frac{14{,}300}{71.5} = 200\). The sum asked for is \(14{,}300 + 200 = 14{,}500\); the graduate count is not part of it.
questions.note: Same template as this book's #35 with different numbers — do not place both in one test.

questions.stem: A property owner wants to find the length \(x\), in feet, across a pond as represented in the figure. PR intersects ST at point Q, and angle PTQ is congruent to angle RSQ. The lengths represented by PQ, TQ, QS, and RS were determined to be 4,200 feet, 8,400 feet, 1,400 feet, and 1,600 feet, respectively. What is the value of \(x\)?
questions.whyCorrect: Angles PQT and RQS are vertical angles, so they are congruent, and you are told angle PTQ is congruent to angle RSQ. That makes triangle PTQ similar to triangle RSQ, with P matching R, T matching S, and Q matching Q. The scale factor comes from the pair of corresponding sides you know completely: TQ : SQ = 8,400 : 1,400 = 6. The distance across the pond is PT, which corresponds to RS, so \(x = 6 \times 1{,}600 = 9{,}600\) feet.
questions.note: Figure needed: two segments PR and ST crossing at Q. T is below P on the left (PT spans the pond, labelled x, drawn as a lens/oval shape); S is upper right and R is lower right, so PR runs from upper left down to lower right and ST runs from lower left up to upper right, crossing at Q.
questions.imageAlt: Two straight paths crossing at a labelled point: one runs from P at the upper left down to R at the lower right, the other from T at the lower left up to S at the upper right. A narrow oval marks the pond around segment PT, and the segment SR is drawn on the right.

questions.stem: An object's speed, in meters per hour, is increasing at a rate of 1,490 meters per hour per second. Which of the following is closest to this rate in feet per second squared? (Use 1 meter = 3.28 feet.)
questions.whyCorrect: The starting units are meters per hour per second, so only one of the two time units is an hour. Convert meters to feet: \(1{,}490 \times 3.28 = 4{,}887.2\) feet per hour per second. Then turn that hour into seconds by dividing by 3,600: \(\frac{4887.2}{3600} \approx 1.36\) feet per second squared. Note you divide by 3,600 once, not twice — only one time unit was in hours.

whyWrong.A: This is \(\frac{1490}{3.28 \times 3600}\) — dividing by 3.28 when meters must be multiplied by 3.28 to give feet.
whyWrong.C: This is \(\frac{1490}{3.28 \times 60}\): the length factor inverted and only 60 used for the hour.
whyWrong.D: This is \(\frac{1490 \times 3.28}{60}\), dividing by 60 rather than 3,600. There are 3,600 seconds in an hour.

questions.stem:
In triangle ABC and triangle DEF, sides \( \overline{AB} \) and \( \overline{DE} \) each have a side length of 10 inches, and angles A and D each have an angle measure of 40°. Which of the following additional pieces of information is (are) sufficient to prove whether triangle ABC is congruent to triangle DEF?

I. The measures of angles B and C are equal.
II. The lengths of sides \( \overline{AC} \) and \( \overline{DF} \) are equal.
III. The lengths of sides \( \overline{BC} \) and \( \overline{EF} \) are equal.

choices.label: A
choices.content: I is sufficient, but II and III are not.

choices.label: B
choices.content: II is sufficient, but I and III are not.

choices.label: C
choices.content: III is sufficient, but I and II are not.

choices.label: D
choices.content: II is sufficient and III is sufficient, but I is not.

questions.whyCorrect: Statement II adds the side on the other arm of the 40° angle, so you have side-angle-side with the angle between the two known sides — that fixes the triangle completely, and SAS proves congruence. Statement I only describes triangle ABC and says nothing at all about DEF. Statement III gives side-side-angle, with the equal angle not between the equal sides, which is the ambiguous case: two different triangles can share those measurements.

whyWrong.A: I compares two angles inside the same triangle. It constrains the shape of ABC but tells you nothing about DEF, so it cannot decide congruence.
whyWrong.C: III is SSA. Because BC lies opposite the known 40° angle rather than beside it, two non-congruent triangles can satisfy every stated measurement.
whyWrong.D: II works, but adding III to it is the SSA trap. Only the included-angle version, SAS, is a congruence criterion.

The table shows three values of x and their corresponding values of f(x), where \[ f(x) = \frac{kx + 45}{x + 2} \]and k is a constant. What is the value of k?
questions.whyCorrect: Pick the row that makes the algebra shortest: f(-9) = 0. A fraction is zero only when its numerator is zero, so k(-9) + 45 = 0, giving 9k = 45 and k = 5. You can confirm with another row: \( f(33) = \frac{5(33) + 45}{35} = \frac{210}{35} = 6 \) , as the table says.

questions.stem: One gallon of sealant costs $13 and will cover 300 square feet of a surface. A deck has a total surface area of \( d \) square feet. Which equation represents the cost \( c \), in dollars, of the sealant needed to cover the deck twice?
questions.whyCorrect: Two coats means \( 2d \) square feet must be covered, so the gallons needed are \( \frac{2d}{300} = \frac{d}{150} \). Cost is gallons times price per gallon, so \( c = 13\left(\frac{d}{150}\right) \). Doubling the area halves the denominator, which is why 300 becomes 150.

whyWrong.A: This puts the coverage on top and the price underneath, giving square feet per dollar, and it never accounts for the second coat.
whyWrong.B: Same inverted structure, with the doubling applied to the wrong number.
whyWrong.D: \( 13\left(\frac{d}{300}\right) \) is the cost of a single coat.

questions.note: Same template as expressions-60 and expressions-90 (only the price per gallon and coverage differ); flag the group at allocation.

questions.stem: The function f is a quadratic function. In the xy-plane, the graph of \( y = f(x) \) has a vertex at (1, 9) and passes through the points (2, 33) and (-1, 105). What is the value of \( f(-2) - f(0) \) ?
questions.whyCorrect: Use vertex form: \( f(x) = a(x - 1)^{2} + 9 \) . The point (2, 33) gives \( a(1) + 9 = 33 \) , so a = 24, and (-1, 105) confirms it since \( 24(4) + 9 = 105 \) . Then \( f(-2) = 24(9) + 9 = 225 \) and \( f(0) = 24(1) + 9 = 33 \) , so the difference is 192.

whyWrong.A: 81 comes from a wrong leading coefficient. Pin a down first from the point (2, 33): \( a(2 - 1)^{2} + 9 = 33 \) forces a = 24.
whyWrong.B: 129 is \( 24(5) + 9 \) , which evaluates \( (-2 - 1)^{2} \) as \( (-2)^{2} + 1 \) . Subtract inside the parentheses first: \( (-3)^{2} = 9 \) .
whyWrong.D: 225 is \( f(-2) \) on its own. The question asks for the difference, so \( f(0) = 33 \) still has to come off.

questions.stem: Which equation has no solution?
questions.whyCorrect: Compare the x coefficients first. No solution needs the x terms to match while the constants do not. In choice B both sides have \( -19x \), and adding \( 19x \) leaves \( -\frac{1}{7} = \frac{1}{7} \), which is false, so nothing satisfies it.

whyWrong.A: The two sides are literally identical, so every value of x works — infinitely many solutions.
whyWrong.C: The coefficients differ (\( -19x \) versus \( 19x \)), so the x terms do not cancel; solving gives x = 0.
whyWrong.D: The coefficients differ again, so there is exactly one solution, \( x = -\frac{1}{133} \).

questions.stem: The relationship between the variables x and y is defined by an exponential equation. When x = 0, the value of y is 40, and for every increase in the value of x by 1, the corresponding value of y increases by 50% of its previous value. Which equation represents this relationship?
questions.whyCorrect: Two numbers to place. The value at x = 0 is the coefficient, so it is 40. The 50% growth per step becomes the base 1 + 0.50 = 1.50. Keep them apart: 40 is a starting amount and 50% is a rate.

whyWrong.B: 1.05 is a 5% increase, not 50%. Convert 50% to 0.50 before adding 1.
whyWrong.C: This swaps the two numbers — 50 is the percentage and 40 is the starting value, not the other way round.
whyWrong.D: Both numbers are misplaced and 1.04 corresponds to a 4% increase, which appears nowhere in the stem.

questions.stem: Which system of linear equations has infinitely many solutions?
questions.whyCorrect: Infinitely many solutions means one equation is a constant multiple of the other — every coefficient and the constant must scale by the same factor. In C, multiply x + 2y = 12 by 4: you get 4x + 8y = 48, exactly the second equation. Same line, so every point on it solves the system.

whyWrong.A: The x-coefficients are both 4, so no scaling is happening, yet the y-coefficients differ (2 versus 8). Different slopes means the lines cross once.
whyWrong.B: Same problem in reverse: the x-coefficients match at 1 but the y-coefficients are 2 and 8. Exactly one solution.
whyWrong.D: Here x scales by \(\frac{1}{4}\) but y scales by 4. Nothing scales consistently, so the lines have different slopes and meet at one point.

questions.stem: \[f(x) = \sqrt{5x + 6}\]The function f is defined by the given equation. If \(f(a) = -5a\), where a is a constant, what is the value of a?
questions.whyCorrect: Squaring \(\sqrt{5a+6} = -5a\) gives \(25a^2 - 5a - 6 = 0\), which factors as \((5a-3)(5a+2) = 0\), so \(a = \frac{3}{5}\) or \(a = -\frac{2}{5}\). A square root is never negative, so \(-5a \ge 0\) and a must not be positive. Checking \(a = -\frac{2}{5}\): \(\sqrt{-2+6} = 2\) and \(-5\left(-\frac{2}{5}\right) = 2\).

whyWrong.A: This is the extraneous root that squaring introduces. It makes the right side \(-3\), and \(\sqrt{9} = 3\), not \(-3\).
whyWrong.B: Not a root of \(25a^2 - 5a - 6 = 0\) at all: substituting gives \(-4\), and it is positive, which the sign check already rules out.
whyWrong.D: Also not a root: substituting \(-\frac{3}{5}\) into \(25a^2 - 5a - 6\) gives 6, not 0.

questions.stem: The function f is defined by f(x) = 25x + 70. What is the value of f(x) when x = 2 ?
questions.whyCorrect: Substitute 2 everywhere x appears: f(2) = 25(2) + 70 = 50 + 70 = 120. Multiply before adding.

whyWrong.A: 50 is just 25(2); you stopped before adding the 70.
whyWrong.B: 97 comes from 25 + 70 + 2, adding the input rather than multiplying by it.
whyWrong.D: 190 comes from adding first and then multiplying, (25 + 70)(2), which is the wrong order of operations.
